<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
There is an integer $N_3\ge1$ such that for every $N\ge N_3$ and every odd $d\ge3$ the set $\mathrm{HGAS}(N,d)$ is many-one complete. In particular, for every $N\ge N_3$, no algorithm decides whether the origin of a homogeneous cubic vector field on $\mathbb{R}^N$ with rational coefficients is GAS, and the set of codes of such vector fields whose origin is not GAS is not recursively enumerable.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:cubicization}
Fix $n\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, and put $m=\binom{n+k-1}{k}$. There is a computable map which sends the rational coefficients of a homogeneous vector field $F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ of degree $2k+1$ to the rational coefficients of a homogeneous cubic vector field $H:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m$ such that
\begin{align}
0\text{ is GAS for }\dot x=F(x)&\iff 0\text{ is GAS for }\dot y=H(y),\label{eq:mainGAS}\\
0\text{ is Lyapunov stable for }\dot x=F(x)&\iff 0\text{ is Lyapunov stable for }\dot y=H(y).\label{eq:mainLS}
\end{align}
The map can be chosen uniformly in $(n,k)$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform}).
<!-- end theorem-2 -->

<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:ls-cubic}
There is $m_0\ge1$ such that for every $N\ge m_0$ and every odd $d\ge3$ the set $\mathrm{HLS}(N,d)$ is many-one hard. In particular, Lyapunov stability of the origin is undecidable for homogeneous cubic vector fields with rational coefficients in a fixed dimension, and the set of codes of such vector fields whose origin is not Lyapunov stable is not recursively enumerable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:fixedpair}
There are an integer $N_*\ge1$ and an odd integer $d_*\ge3$ such that $\mathrm{HGAS}(N_*,d_*)$ is many-one complete.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:variable}
The sets $\mathrm{HGAS}$, $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,3)$ and $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)$, $d\ge3$ odd, are many-one complete. Their complements are not recursively enumerable.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:tarski}
There is a Turing machine which, given a sentence, halts and outputs $1$ if the sentence is true and $0$ if it is false.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:scaling}
For a homogeneous polynomial vector field $f$, the origin is Lyapunov stable if and only if there is $C<\infty$ such that every solution of \eqref{eq:intro-ode} exists for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|x(t)\|\le C\|x(0)\|$ for all $t\ge0$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:even}
No homogeneous vector field $f\ne0$ of even degree $d$ has an asymptotically stable origin. Indeed $f(-x)=f(x)$. If $x(t)=\phi(t,x_0)\to0$ for some $x_0\ne0$, then for every $T>0$ the path $y(s)=-x(T-s)$, $0\le s\le T$, satisfies $\dot y=f(y)$, so $\phi(T,-x(T))=-x_0$. As $T\to\infty$ the initial points $-x(T)$ tend to zero while their images at time $T$ have norm $|x_0|$, contradicting Lyapunov stability. The zero vector field is not GAS either. The obstruction concerns asymptotic stability only: the quadratic vector field $(-x_2x_3,\,x_1x_3,\,0)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ rotates each plane $\{x_3=c\}$ with angular speed $c$ and preserves $|x|$, so its origin is Lyapunov stable.

In dimension one every homogeneous vector field is $\dot x=ax^d$. Its origin is GAS exactly when $d$ is odd and $a<0$, and Lyapunov stable exactly when $a=0$, or $d$ is odd and $a<0$. Hence the one-dimensional problems are decidable, uniformly in $d$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:blocks}
Let $a\in C(\mathcal{K})$ and $M(T)=\max_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\int_0^Ta(\varphi_tx)\,dt$ for $T>0$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blocks-limit}
\beta(\varphi,a)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{M(T)}{T}=\inf_{T>0}\frac{M(T)}{T}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\beta(\varphi,a)<0$ if and only if there are $T,c>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blocks}
\int_0^Ta(\varphi_tx)\,dt\le-c\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal{K}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The flow property gives $\int_0^{S+T}a(\varphi_tx)\,dt=\int_0^Sa(\varphi_tx)\,dt+\int_0^Ta(\varphi_t\varphi_Sx)\,dt$, so $M(S+T)\le M(S)+M(T)$. Put $M(0)=0$. Then $M$ is continuous and subadditive on $[0,\infty)$, and $M(T)\ge-T\max|a|$, so by Fekete's lemma \cite[Chapter~16, Theorem~16.2.9 and (16.2.10), pp.~463--464, and the remark on p.~465 for functions on $[0,\infty)$]{Kuczma} the limit $\lim_{T\to\infty}M(T)/T$ exists, equals $\inf_{T>0}M(T)/T$, and is finite. If $\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\varphi)$ and $T>0$, then invariance and Fubini's theorem give $\int a\,d\mu=\frac1T\int\int_0^Ta(\varphi_tx)\,dt\,d\mu(x)\le M(T)/T$; hence $\beta(\varphi,a)\le\inf M(T)/T$. Conversely, choose $T_j\to\infty$ and $x_j\in\mathcal{K}$ with $M(T_j)=\int_0^{T_j}a(\varphi_tx_j)\,dt$, and let $\mu_j$ be the probability measure $g\mapsto\frac1{T_j}\int_0^{T_j}g(\varphi_tx_j)\,dt$. By weak-star compactness a subsequence converges to a probability measure $\mu$. For $s\in\mathbb{R}$ and $g\in C(\mathcal{K})$ we have $\bigl|\int g\circ\varphi_s\,d\mu_j-\int g\,d\mu_j\bigr|\le2|s|\max|g|/T_j\to0$, so $\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\varphi)$, and $\int a\,d\mu=\lim M(T_j)/T_j$. This proves \eqref{eq:blocks-limit}. If $\beta(\varphi,a)<0$, some $T$ has $M(T)<0$, which is \eqref{eq:blocks} with $c=-M(T)$. Conversely \eqref{eq:blocks} gives $M(T)/T\le-c/T<0$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:lyap}
The origin is Lyapunov stable for $\dot y=P(y)$ if and only if $M_P^*<\infty$. In that case every solution is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|y(t)\|_Q\le e^{M_P^*}\|y(0)\|_Q$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The linear map $z=M^{1/2}y$ is an isometry from $(\mathbb{R}^s,\|\cdot\|_Q)$ onto Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^s$, maps $S_Q$ onto $S^{s-1}$, and transforms $\dot y=P(y)$ into $\dot z=\tilde P(z):=M^{1/2}P(M^{-1/2}z)$, which is homogeneous of degree $D$. In the notation of \cite[Section~2]{Korda}, a direct computation gives $\lambda_{\tilde P}(M^{1/2}u)=a_P(u)$ and $\tilde P^\top(M^{1/2}u)=M^{1/2}Y_P(u)$ for $u\in S_Q$, so $M^{1/2}$ conjugates $\Phi_P$ to the flow of $\tilde P^\top$ on the unit sphere and preserves the integrals $A_P$. In particular $M_P^*$ equals the quantity $M_{\tilde P}$ of \cite[Lemma~2.2]{Korda}. Lyapunov stability is invariant under linear changes of coordinates, so the lemma is \cite[Lemma~2.2]{Korda} applied to $\tilde P$, and the bound on $\|y(t)\|_Q$ is the bound $r(t)\le e^{M_{\tilde P}}r_0$ established in its proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:gascrit}
The origin is GAS for $\dot y=P(y)$ if and only if $\beta(\Phi_P,a_P)<0$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose $\beta(\Phi_P,a_P)<0$, and let $T,c>0$ be given by Lemma~\ref{lem:blocks}; put $A=\max_{S_Q}|a_P|$. Writing $\tau=kT+\sigma$ with $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0\le\sigma<T$, the cocycle identity gives $A_P(u,\tau)\le-kc+AT\le AT+c-c\tau/T$ for all $u\in S_Q$ and $\tau\ge0$. By \eqref{eq:polarsol}, a solution with $y(0)=r_0u_0$ satisfies $r(t)\le r_0e^{AT+c}e^{-c\tau(t)/T}$ on its maximal interval $[0,t_+)$. In particular $y$ is bounded, so $t_+=\infty$ by Section~\ref{subsec:ode}, and the origin is Lyapunov stable. The angular time $\tau$ is increasing. If $\tau(t)\le\tau_1$ for all $t\ge0$, then \eqref{eq:polarsol} gives $r(t)\ge r_0e^{-A\tau_1}$, hence $\tau(t)\ge(r_0e^{-A\tau_1})^{D-1}t\to\infty$, a contradiction. Thus $\tau(t)\to\infty$, and $r(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

Conversely, suppose the origin is GAS. Rosier's homogeneous converse theorem \cite[Theorem~2, p.~468]{Rosier} supplies a $C^1$ function $V$ on $\mathbb{R}^s$, positive away from $0$ and homogeneous of some degree $\ell>0$, with $\nabla V(y)\cdot P(y)<0$ for $y\ne0$. By compactness of $S_Q$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $b(u):=\nabla V(u)\cdot P(u)/V(u)\le-\varepsilon$ on $S_Q$. Euler's identity $\nabla V(u)\cdot u=\ell V(u)$ \cite[Chapter~9, Section~9.3, Exercise~8, p.~287]{Apostol} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:euler}
\nabla(\log V)(u)\cdot Y_P(u)=b(u)-\ell\,a_P(u)\qquad(u\in S_Q).
\end{equation}
By \ref{E:deriv} the left side has integral zero against every $\mu\in\mathcal{M}(\Phi_P)$, so $\ell\int a_P\,d\mu=\int b\,d\mu\le-\varepsilon$, and $\beta(\Phi_P,a_P)\le-\varepsilon/\ell<0$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:compare}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:blocks}, $\beta(\Phi_P,a_P)=\lim_{T\to\infty}M_P(T)/T$, so both criteria concern the same function $M_P$: the origin is Lyapunov stable if and only if $M_P$ is bounded, and GAS if and only if $M_P(T)<0$ for some $T>0$. In particular Lyapunov stability implies $\beta(\Phi_P,a_P)\le0$. Invariant averages cannot detect Lyapunov stability, however. The cubic vector fields $P_1(y)=|y|^2(-y_2,y_1)$ and $P_2(y)=|y|^2(y_2,0)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ both have $\beta=0$ with respect to $Q(y)=|y|^2$: for $P_1$ because $a_{P_1}\equiv0$, and for $P_2$ because the only zeros of its angular vector field are $\pm(1,0)$, where $a_{P_2}=0$, and every other angular orbit is a heteroclinic arc, which carries no invariant probability measure. The origin is Lyapunov stable for $P_1$, which preserves $|y|$, but not for $P_2$, whose solutions with $y_2(0)\ne0$ blow up in finite time. This is why the Lyapunov half of Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization} needs a statement about individual trajectories (Proposition~\ref{prop:shadow}).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:re}
$\mathrm{HGAS}$ is recursively enumerable. Consequently so are $\mathrm{HGAS}(n,d)$ and $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)$ for all fixed $n,d$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Given a code $e$, first decide whether it is valid, and reject it if not. For a valid code, decide $D(e,0),D(e,1),\dots$ in turn by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski}, and accept as soon as one of them is true. We show that $e\in\mathrm{HGAS}$ if and only if $D(e,r)$ holds for some $r$.

If $D(e,r)$ holds, compactness of $S^{n-1}$ and homogeneity give $m_0,M_0,\mu_0>0$ with $m_0|x|^2\le V(x)\le M_0|x|^2$ and $-\nabla V(x)\cdot f(x)\ge\mu_0|x|^{d+1}$ for $x\ne0$. The extension $V(0)=0$ is $C^1$, since $V=O(|x|^2)$ and $\nabla V=O(|x|)$. Along a solution, $V$ is nonincreasing, so every solution stays in a compact sublevel set and exists for all $t\ge0$, and the origin is Lyapunov stable. Moreover $\mu_0\int_0^\infty|x(t)|^{d+1}dt\le V(x(0))<\infty$, and $|x(t)|^{d+1}$ is uniformly continuous because $\dot x$ is bounded; by Barbalat's lemma \cite[Chapter~8, Lemma~8.2, p.~323]{Khalil}, $x(t)\to0$.

Conversely, if the origin is GAS, then by \cite[Theorem~3.1]{AEK} there are $r\in\mathbb{N}$ and a positive definite homogeneous polynomial $p$ of degree $2r+2$ (with real coefficients) such that \eqref{eq:Vp} is a strict Lyapunov function, that is, $\nabla V(x)\cdot f(x)<0$ for $x\ne0$. Then $D(e,r)$ holds. The statements for fixed $n,d$ follow by \ref{C:trans}, since $\mathrm{HGAS}(n,d)$ and $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)$ are preimages of $\mathrm{HGAS}$ under computable maps of codes.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:contrast}
Proposition~\ref{prop:re} has no known analogue for Lyapunov stability. The reduction of \cite{Korda} is a computable map $n\mapsto F_n$ with ``$\mathsf U$ halts on $n$ $\iff$ the origin is Lyapunov stable for $F_n$'' \cite[(1.1)]{Korda}. When the halting set of $\mathsf U$ is many-one complete, as for the machine of \cite[Remark~3.2]{Korda}, the Lyapunov stable codes form a many-one hard set in the dimension and degree of \cite{Korda}, so the codes whose origin is \emph{not} Lyapunov stable cannot be enumerated (Section~\ref{subsec:computability} and Corollary~\ref{cor:ls-cubic}). For homogeneous vector fields, positive instances of GAS can therefore be certified, whereas negative instances of Lyapunov stability cannot. The converse theorem behind Proposition~\ref{prop:re} uses asymptotic stability and homogeneity in an essential way \cite{AEK}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:binary}
For $n=k=2$ we have $\nu_2(x_1,x_2)=(x_1^2,x_1x_2,x_2^2)$, $Q=y_{20}^2+2y_{11}^2+y_{02}^2$, a single binomial $q=y_{20}y_{02}-y_{11}^2$, $W=q^2$, and $\operatorname{grad}_Q W=M^{-1}\nabla W=(2qy_{02},\,-2qy_{11},\,2qy_{20})$, which is cubic. Since the Veronese relations are quadratic, the gradient of the quartic $W$ has exactly the degree we want.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:local}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem $V\setminus\{0\}\subseteq U_1\cup\dots\cup U_n$.
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem Let $1\le i\le n$. For $y\in U_i$ define $\xi=\xi^{(i)}(y)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ by $\xi_i=1$ and $\xi_j=y_{(k-1)e_i+e_j}/y_{ke_i}$ for $j\ne i$, and put $\pi_i(y)=y_{ke_i}\,\nu_k(\xi)$. Then $\pi_i(y)\in V$, the coordinates of $\pi_i(y)$ indexed by $B_i$ agree with those of $y$, and there is a continuous function $\kappa_i:U_i\to[0,\infty)$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E4}
\|y-\pi_i(y)\|_Q\le\kappa_i(y)\,W(y)^{1/2}\qquad(y\in U_i).
\end{equation}
In particular every $y\in V\cap U_i$ satisfies $y=\pi_i(y)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(a) Let $y\in V\setminus\{0\}$. Since $y\ne0$ and $k\ge1$, there are $i$ and $\alpha\in A_k$ with $y_\alpha\ne0$ and $\alpha_i\ge1$; among all such pairs choose one with $\alpha_i$ maximal. If $\alpha\ne ke_i$, pick $j\ne i$ with $\alpha_j\ge1$. Since \eqref{eq:E2} vanishes at $y$, $y_{\alpha+e_i-e_j}y_{\alpha-e_i+e_j}=y_\alpha^2\ne0$, so $y_{\alpha+e_i-e_j}\ne0$, contradicting the maximality of $\alpha_i$. Hence $\alpha=ke_i$ and $y\in U_i$.

(b) Let $N_i=A_k\setminus B_i$, so $\#N_i=m-n$, and write $y_N=(y_\alpha)_{\alpha\in N_i}$. Each $\alpha\in N_i$ has $\alpha_i\le k-2$, so we may fix $j_\alpha\ne i$ with $\alpha_{j_\alpha}\ge1$ and set $\alpha'=\alpha+e_i-e_{j_\alpha}\in A_k$. The polynomial $r_\alpha=y_{ke_i}y_\alpha-y_{(k-1)e_i+e_{j_\alpha}}y_{\alpha'}$ is of type \eqref{eq:E3}, so it vanishes on $V$ and $r_\alpha^2\le W$. Its coefficients are coordinates indexed by $B_i$, and $\alpha'$ lies either in $B_i$ or in $N_i$. Hence the vector $r=(r_\alpha)_{\alpha\in N_i}$ has the form $r(y)=L_i(y)\,y_N-\ell_i(y)$, where the square matrix $L_i(y)$ and the vector $\ell_i(y)$ depend only on the coordinates indexed by $B_i$, all diagonal entries of $L_i(y)$ equal $y_{ke_i}$, and its only other nonzero entries are $-y_{(k-1)e_i+e_{j_\alpha}}$ in the positions $(\alpha,\alpha')$ with $\alpha'\in N_i$. If $N_i$ is ordered by nonincreasing $\alpha_i$, these positions lie below the diagonal, since $\alpha'_i=\alpha_i+1$. Thus $\det L_i(y)=y_{ke_i}^{m-n}$, and by the adjugate formula for the inverse \cite[Chapter~6, (6.2.7), p.~479]{Meyer} the function $\kappa_i(y):=\sqrt{k!(m-n)}\,\|L_i(y)^{-1}\|$ (operator norm) is continuous on $U_i$.

Let $y\in U_i$ and $\pi=\pi_i(y)$. Since $\pi_{ke_i}=y_{ke_i}\xi_i^k=y_{ke_i}$ and $\pi_{(k-1)e_i+e_j}=y_{ke_i}\xi_j=y_{(k-1)e_i+e_j}$, the point $\pi$ agrees with $y$ in the coordinates indexed by $B_i$, and $\pi\in V$ by \eqref{eq:E1}. Hence $0=r(\pi)=L_i(y)\pi_N-\ell_i(y)$, so $r(y)=L_i(y)(y_N-\pi_N)$. As $y-\pi$ vanishes in the coordinates indexed by $B_i$ and $|r(y)|^2\le(m-n)W(y)$,
\[
\|y-\pi\|_Q\le\sqrt{k!}\,|y_N-\pi_N|\le\sqrt{k!}\,\|L_i(y)^{-1}\|\,|r(y)|\le\kappa_i(y)\,W(y)^{1/2}.
\]
If $y\in V$, then $W(y)=0$ and $y=\pi$. (If $N_i=\emptyset$, then $y=\pi$ and $\kappa_i=0$.)
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:cone}
The nonzero points of $V$ are exactly the points $t\,\nu_k(u)$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ and $u\in S^{n-1}$. Consequently $\Sigma=\{\sigma\nu_k(u):\sigma\in\{-1,1\},\ u\in S^{n-1}\}$, and $\Sigma$ is a compact subset of $S_Q$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If $t\ne0$ and $u\in S^{n-1}$, then $t\nu_k(u)\in V$ by \eqref{eq:E1}, and $Q(t\nu_k(u))=t^2$ by \eqref{eq:Qnu}, so $t\nu_k(u)\ne0$. Conversely, if $y\in V\setminus\{0\}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:local} gives $i$ with $y\in U_i$ and $y=c\,\nu_k(\xi)$, where $c=y_{ke_i}\ne0$ and $\xi\ne0$; as $\nu_k(sx)=s^k\nu_k(x)$, this is $t\nu_k(u)$ with $t=c|\xi|^k$ and $u=\xi/|\xi|$. Since $Q(t\nu_k(u))=t^2$, such a point lies on $S_Q$ if and only if $t=\pm1$, and $\Sigma$ is compact as a continuous image of $\{-1,1\}\times S^{n-1}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:dist}
For $y\in S_Q$ let $d(y)=\min_{p\in\Sigma}\|y-p\|_Q$. There is $c_1>0$ such that $W(y)\ge c_1\,d(y)^2$ for all $y\in S_Q$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The minimum exists since $\Sigma$ is compact and nonempty, and $d\le2$ on $S_Q$. Put $\delta=\frac12n^{-k/2}$. Each $p=\sigma\nu_k(u)\in\Sigma$ has $|p_{ke_i}|=|u_i|^k\ge2\delta$ for every $i$ with $|u_i|\ge n^{-1/2}$, and such $i$ exist since $|u|=1$. Hence the compact set $K_0=\{y\in S_Q:\max_i|y_{ke_i}|\le\delta\}$ does not meet $\Sigma$, which is the zero set of $W$ on $S_Q$; so if $K_0\ne\emptyset$, then $w_0=\min_{K_0}W>0$ and $W\ge\frac{w_0}4d^2$ on $K_0$. Every other $y\in S_Q$ lies in one of the compact sets $K_i=\{y\in S_Q:|y_{ke_i}|\ge\delta\}\subseteq U_i$; let $C_i>0$ be an upper bound for $\kappa_i$ on $K_i$. For $y\in K_i$, the point $\pi=\pi_i(y)$ is nonzero, $p=\pi/\|\pi\|_Q$ lies in $V\cap S_Q=\Sigma$ by \eqref{eq:E1}, and $\bigl|\|\pi\|_Q-1\bigr|\le\|y-\pi\|_Q$ because $\|y\|_Q=1$. By \eqref{eq:E4},
\[
d(y)\le\|y-p\|_Q\le\|y-\pi\|_Q+\bigl|\|\pi\|_Q-1\bigr|\le2\|y-\pi\|_Q\le2C_i\,W(y)^{1/2}.
\]
Thus $c_1=\min\{w_0/4,(4C_1^2)^{-1},\dots,(4C_n^2)^{-1}\}$ works (omit $w_0/4$ if $K_0=\emptyset$).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:gradineq}
There are computable positive rationals $\eta,c$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gradineq}
Q(y)=1,\ W(y)\le\eta\implies D(y)\ge c\,W(y).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $c_1$ and $d$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:dist}, let $L=\max\{|q_j(h)|:1\le j\le s,\ Q(h)=1\}$ (and $L=0$ if $s=0$), so that $|q_j(h)|\le L\|h\|_Q^2$ for $h\in E$, and put $\rho=\min\{\frac12,\sqrt{c_1}/(2(L\sqrt s+1))\}$. We first show
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E5}
y\in S_Q,\ d(y)\le\rho\implies D(y)\ge\tfrac{c_1}{4}W(y).
\end{equation}
If $y\in\Sigma$, then $W(y)=0$ and \eqref{eq:E5} is trivial. Otherwise choose $p\in\Sigma$ with $\|y-p\|_Q=d:=d(y)>0$ and put $h=y-p$. Every homogeneous quadratic polynomial $q$ on $E$ satisfies $q(a+b)=q(a)+Dq(a)b+q(b)$, as one sees by writing $q(y)=y^TAy$ with $A$ symmetric. With $a=y$, $b=-h$ and $q_j(p)=0$ this gives $Dq_j(y)h=q_j(y)+q_j(h)$. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, $d\le(W(y)/c_1)^{1/2}$ and $d\le\rho$,
\[
DW(y)h=2W(y)+2\sum_jq_j(y)q_j(h)\ge2W(y)-2L\sqrt s\,d^2W(y)^{1/2}\ge2\Bigl(1-\frac{L\sqrt s\,d}{\sqrt{c_1}}\Bigr)W(y)\ge W(y).
\]
Let $w=h-\langle y,h\rangle_Qy$, so that $\langle y,w\rangle_Q=0$ and $\|w\|_Q\le d$. As $Q(y)=Q(p)=1$, we have $\langle y,h\rangle_Q=\frac12d^2$, and Euler's identity $DW(y)y=4W(y)$ gives $DW(y)w\ge(1-2d^2)W(y)\ge\frac12W(y)$. On the other hand $DW(y)w=\langle\operatorname{grad}_{S_Q} W(y),w\rangle_Q\le D(y)^{1/2}d$. Hence $D(y)\ge W(y)^2/(4d^2)\ge\frac{c_1}{4}W(y)$, proving \eqref{eq:E5}.

The set $K_\rho=\{y\in S_Q:d(y)\ge\rho\}$ is compact and disjoint from $\Sigma$, so there is $\eta_0>0$ with $W\ge2\eta_0$ on $K_\rho$ (any $\eta_0>0$ if $K_\rho=\emptyset$). If $y\in S_Q$ and $W(y)\le\eta_0$, then $d(y)<\rho$ and \eqref{eq:E5} applies. Thus \eqref{eq:gradineq} holds for $(\eta_0,c_1/4)$, and hence for every rational pair $(\eta,c)$ with $0<\eta\le\eta_0$ and $0<c\le c_1/4$, because decreasing $\eta$ strengthens the hypothesis and decreasing $c$ weakens the conclusion. To compute such a pair, enumerate pairs of positive rationals and decide for each the sentence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QEgrad}
\forall y\ \ \bigl(Q(y)=1\wedge W(y)\le\eta\bigr)\implies D(y)\ge c\,W(y)
\end{equation}
by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski}, stopping at the first true one; by what we have shown, the search terminates.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:tangency}
For the rational $\eta$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:gradineq} one can compute rationals $C_F,A_F>0$ such that
\begin{align}
Q(y)=1,\ W(y)\le\eta&\implies|Y_GW(y)|\le C_F\,W(y),\label{eq:tangency}\\
Q(y)=1&\implies|a_G(y)|\le A_F,\label{eq:AF}
\end{align}
where $Y_GW(y)=DW(y)Y_G(y)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $c_1$ and $d$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:dist}, and put $\psi_j(y)=Dq_j(y)Y_G(y)$. Since $q_j$ and $\psi_j$ are polynomials, their derivatives are bounded on the open convex set $\{Q<2\}$, so the mean value inequality \cite[Chapter~9, Theorem~9.19, p.~218]{Rudin} on this set and the equivalence of the norms $|\cdot|$ and $\|\cdot\|_Q$ give $L'>0$ with $|q_j(y)-q_j(y')|\le L'\|y-y'\|_Q$ and $|\psi_j(y)-\psi_j(y')|\le L'\|y-y'\|_Q$ for $y,y'\in\{Q\le1\}$. For $y\in S_Q$ choose $p\in\Sigma$ with $\|y-p\|_Q=d(y)$. As $q_j(p)=0$ and $\psi_j(p)=0$ by \eqref{eq:E7}, the identity $Y_GW=2\sum_jq_j\psi_j$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:dist} give
\[
|Y_GW(y)|\le2sL'^2d(y)^2\le\frac{2sL'^2}{c_1}W(y)\qquad(y\in S_Q).
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:tangency} holds for some real constant, and then for every larger rational. To compute one, enumerate positive rationals $C$ and decide by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski} the sentence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QEtan}
\forall y\ \ \bigl(Q(y)=1\wedge W(y)\le\eta\bigr)\implies\bigl(Y_GW(y)\bigr)^2\le C^2W(y)^2;
\end{equation}
the search terminates. Similarly, $a_G$ is bounded on the compact set $S_Q$, and a rational $A_F$ is found by deciding $\forall y\,(Q(y)=1\Rightarrow a_G(y)^2\le A^2)$ for $A=1,2,\dots$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:lipschitz}
One can compute a rational $L_G>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:LG}
\|Y_G(y)-Y_G(y')\|_Q\le L_G\|y-y'\|_Q,\qquad|a_G(y)-a_G(y')|\le L_G\|y-y'\|_Q
\end{equation}
whenever $Q(y)\le1$ and $Q(y')\le1$. Moreover the flow $\phi^G_t$ of $Y_G$ on $S_Q$ is defined for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
$Y_G$ and $a_G$ are polynomial maps, so, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:tangency}, the mean value inequality on $\{Q<2\}$ gives a real constant with \eqref{eq:LG}, and then every larger rational works; a rational one is found by enumerating rationals $L$ and deciding
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall y,y'\ \ \bigl(Q(y)\le1\wedge Q(y')\le1\bigr)\implies\Bigl(&Q\bigl(Y_G(y)-Y_G(y')\bigr)\le L^2Q(y-y')\\
&\wedge\bigl(a_G(y)-a_G(y')\bigr)^2\le L^2Q(y-y')\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
By Section~\ref{sec:angular}, the compact set $S_Q$ is invariant under $Y_G$, so $\phi^G_t$ is a flow on $S_Q$ (Section~\ref{subsec:ode}).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:conedyn}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem For $u\in S^{n-1}$, $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:E8}
\phi^H_t(\sigma\nu_k(u))=\phi^G_t(\sigma\nu_k(u))=\sigma\nu_k(\phi^F_t(u)),\qquad a_H(\sigma\nu_k(u))=k\,a_F(u).
\end{equation}
Consequently $\phi^H_t(\Sigma)=\Sigma$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:AHcone}
A_H(\sigma\nu_k(u),\tau)=k\,A_F(u,\tau),\qquad\max_{p\in\Sigma}A_H(p,\tau)=k\,M_F(\tau)\qquad(\tau\ge0).
\end{equation}
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem If $x(t)$ solves $\dot x=F(x)$ on an interval, then $y(t)=\nu_k(x(t))$ solves $\dot y=H(y)$ on the same interval, and $\|y(t)\|_Q=|x(t)|^k$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(a) On $V$ we have $W=0$ and $H=G$, so $a_H=a_G$ and $Y_H=Y_G$ on $\Sigma$ by \eqref{eq:aH}. For $u\in S^{n-1}$ and $\sigma=\pm1$, the curve $c(t)=\sigma\nu_k(\phi^F_t(u))$ lies in $\Sigma$ and, by \eqref{eq:aGnu} and the oddness of $Y_G$, satisfies $c'(t)=\sigma Y_G(\nu_k(\phi^F_tu))=Y_G(c(t))=Y_H(c(t))$. Uniqueness of solutions gives the first identity in \eqref{eq:E8}, and \eqref{eq:aGnu} with the evenness of $a_G$ gives the second. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cone} every point of $\Sigma$ has the form $\sigma\nu_k(u)$, so $\phi^H_t(\Sigma)=\Sigma$. Integrating the second identity in \eqref{eq:E8} along the first gives \eqref{eq:AHcone}.

(b) By \eqref{eq:Gnu}, $\dot y=D\nu_k(x)F(x)=G(\nu_k(x))=G(y)$, and $G(y)=H(y)$ because $y\in V$ by \eqref{eq:E1}. Finally $\|y\|_Q^2=Q(\nu_k(x))=|x|^{2k}$ by \eqref{eq:Qnu}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:tube}
Let $\lambda=Kc-C_F$, so that $\lambda\ge2L_G+1$ by \eqref{eq:Kchoice}, and let $\mathcal{T}=\{y\in S_Q:W(y)\le\eta\}$. Then $a_H<-1$ on $S_Q\setminus\mathcal{T}$. Moreover $\mathcal{T}$ is forward invariant under $\phi^H$, and $W(\phi^H_ty)\le W(y)e^{-\lambda t}$ for $y\in\mathcal{T}$ and $t\ge0$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
On $\mathcal{T}$, Lemmas~\ref{lem:gradineq} and~\ref{lem:tangency} and \eqref{eq:aH} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tubedecay}
Y_HW\le C_FW-KcW=-\lambda W.
\end{equation}
Hence the function $w(t)=W(\phi^H_ty)$ satisfies $w'\le-\lambda w$ as long as $w(t)\le\eta$; this implies that $\mathcal{T}$ is forward invariant and, by Gronwall's inequality, that $w(t)\le w(0)e^{-\lambda t}$. If $y\in S_Q\setminus\mathcal{T}$, then $W(y)>\eta$, and \eqref{eq:AF}, \eqref{eq:Kchoice} and \eqref{eq:aH} give $a_H(y)\le A_F-4K\eta<-1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:dichotomy}
Let $\mu$ be an ergodic invariant probability measure for $\phi^H$. Then either $\mu(\Sigma)=1$, or $\int a_H\,d\mu\le-1$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The set $\mathcal{T}$ is closed and forward invariant, so $\phi^H_t(\mathcal{T})\subseteq\mathcal{T}$ for $t\ge0$ and invariance of $\mu$ gives $\mu(\mathcal{T}\setminus\phi^H_t(\mathcal{T}))=0$; hence $\mathcal{T}$ is invariant modulo $\mu$-null sets and $\mu(\mathcal{T})\in\{0,1\}$ by ergodicity. If $\mu(\mathcal{T})=1$, then \ref{E:deriv} and \eqref{eq:tubedecay} give $0=\int Y_HW\,d\mu\le-\lambda\int W\,d\mu$, so $W=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere and $\mu(\Sigma)=1$. If $\mu(\mathcal{T})=0$, then $a_H<-1$ $\mu$-almost everywhere by Lemma~\ref{lem:tube}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:coneavg}
Let $\beta_F=\beta(\phi^F,a_F)$ and $\beta_H=\beta(\phi^H,a_H)$. The largest $a_H$-average among measures in $\mathcal{M}(\phi^H)$ supported on $\Sigma$ is $k\beta_F$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sandwich}
k\beta_F\le\beta_H\le\max\{k\beta_F,-1\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:conedyn}(a), $\Sigma$ is a compact invariant set and $\max_{p\in\Sigma}A_H(p,T)=kM_F(T)$ for every $T>0$. The measures in $\mathcal{M}(\phi^H)$ supported on $\Sigma$ are exactly the invariant probability measures of the restricted flow $\phi^H|_\Sigma$. Dividing by $T$ and letting $T\to\infty$, Lemma~\ref{lem:blocks} applied to $(\phi^H|_\Sigma,a_H|_\Sigma)$ and to $(\phi^F,a_F)$ shows that the largest such average is $k\beta_F$. This gives the lower bound in \eqref{eq:sandwich}, and \ref{E:decomp} with Lemma~\ref{lem:dichotomy} gives the upper bound.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:shadow}
There is $C_*>0$ such that for every $y_0\in\mathcal{T}$ and every $\tau\ge0$ there is $q\in\Sigma$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:shadow}
\|\phi^H_t(y_0)-\phi^G_t(q)\|_Q\le C_*e^{-\lambda t/2}\quad(0\le t\le\tau),\qquad A_H(y_0,\tau)\le A_H(q,\tau)+C_*.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: a bound for the penalty.} Since $\langle\operatorname{grad}_Q W(y),y\rangle_Q=4W(y)$ and $Q(y)=1$, the vector $\operatorname{grad}_{S_Q} W(y)$ is the $Q$-orthogonal projection of $\operatorname{grad}_Q W(y)$ onto the $Q$-orthogonal complement of $y$. Hence, with $\Gamma=\max_j\max_{S_Q}\|\operatorname{grad}_Q q_j\|_Q$ (taking $\Gamma=0$ if $s=0$) and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, for $y\in S_Q$,
\[
\|\operatorname{grad}_{S_Q} W(y)\|_Q\le\|\operatorname{grad}_Q W(y)\|_Q=\Bigl\|2\sum_jq_j(y)\operatorname{grad}_Q q_j(y)\Bigr\|_Q\le2\Gamma\sqrt s\,W(y)^{1/2}=:C_WW(y)^{1/2}.
\]

\emph{Step 2: the trajectory is an approximate trajectory of $Y_G$.} Let $y(t)=\phi^H_t(y_0)$ for $t\ge0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tube}, $W(y(t))\le\eta e^{-\lambda t}$. By \eqref{eq:aH} and Step~1, with $\theta_1=KC_W\eta^{1/2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sh1}
y'(t)=Y_G(y(t))+\epsilon(t),\qquad\|\epsilon(t)\|_Q\le\theta_1e^{-\lambda t/2},
\end{equation}
where $\epsilon(t)=-K\operatorname{grad}_{S_Q} W(y(t))$.

\emph{Step 3: the comparison trajectory.} Fix $\tau\ge0$, and let $d$ and $c_1$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:dist}. There is $p\in\Sigma$ with $\|y(\tau)-p\|_Q=d(y(\tau))\le(W(y(\tau))/c_1)^{1/2}\le\theta_0e^{-\lambda\tau/2}$, where $\theta_0=(\eta/c_1)^{1/2}$. Put $z(t)=\phi^G_{t-\tau}(p)$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $q=z(0)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:conedyn}(a), $z(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t$; in particular $q\in\Sigma$, and $\phi^G_t(q)=z(t)$.

\emph{Step 4: the error decays.} Let $e(t)=y(t)-z(t)$ and $r(t)=\|e(t)\|_Q$ for $0\le t\le\tau$. Both $y(t)$ and $z(t)$ lie in $S_Q$, so \eqref{eq:LG} and \eqref{eq:sh1} give $\|e'(t)\|_Q\le L_Gr(t)+\theta_1e^{-\lambda t/2}$. Writing $e(t)=e(s)-\int_t^se'(\sigma)\,d\sigma$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sh2}
r(t)\le r(s)+\int_t^s\bigl(L_Gr(\sigma)+\theta_1e^{-\lambda\sigma/2}\bigr)\,d\sigma\qquad(0\le t\le s\le\tau).
\end{equation}
Let $D=2\theta_0+2\theta_1+1$ and $R(t)=De^{-\lambda t/2}$. Since $\lambda\ge2L_G+1$, we have $(\lambda/2-L_G)R(\sigma)\ge\frac D2e^{-\lambda\sigma/2}>\theta_1e^{-\lambda\sigma/2}$, that is,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sh3}
L_GR(\sigma)+\theta_1e^{-\lambda\sigma/2}<\tfrac\lambda2R(\sigma)=-R'(\sigma)\qquad(\sigma\in\mathbb{R}).
\end{equation}
We claim that $r\le R$ on $[0,\tau]$. Otherwise the closed set $\{t\in[0,\tau]:r(t)\ge R(t)\}$ is nonempty; let $t_1$ be its largest element. Since $r(\tau)\le\theta_0e^{-\lambda\tau/2}<R(\tau)$, we have $t_1<\tau$ and $r<R$ on $(t_1,\tau]$. Then \eqref{eq:sh2} with $t=t_1$, $s=\tau$, and \eqref{eq:sh3} give
\[
r(t_1)\le R(\tau)+\int_{t_1}^\tau\bigl(L_GR(\sigma)+\theta_1e^{-\lambda\sigma/2}\bigr)\,d\sigma<R(\tau)-\int_{t_1}^\tau R'(\sigma)\,d\sigma=R(t_1),
\]
a contradiction. Hence $\|\phi^H_t(y_0)-\phi^G_t(q)\|_Q=r(t)\le De^{-\lambda t/2}$ for $0\le t\le\tau$.

\emph{Step 5: the radial rates.} On $\Sigma$ we have $a_H=a_G$ and $\phi^H_t=\phi^G_t$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:conedyn}(a)), so $A_H(q,\tau)=\int_0^\tau a_G(z(t))\,dt$. By \eqref{eq:aH}, $a_H\le a_G$ on $S_Q$. Hence, by \eqref{eq:LG} and Step~4,
\[
A_H(y_0,\tau)-A_H(q,\tau)\le\int_0^\tau\bigl|a_G(y(t))-a_G(z(t))\bigr|\,dt\le L_GD\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t/2}\,dt=\frac{2L_GD}{\lambda}\le2L_GD.
\]
Thus $C_*=(1+2L_G)D$ works; it depends neither on $y_0$ nor on $\tau$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
If $k=1$, take $H=F$. For $k\ge2$, construct $Q,W,G,K,H$ by \eqref{eq:Q}--\eqref{eq:H}. Every step is effective: the binomials \eqref{eq:binom} are a finite explicit list, $G$ is obtained by expanding $D\nu_k(x)F(x)$ and factoring monomials, the rationals $\eta,c,C_F,A_F,L_G$ are found by the terminating searches in Lemmas~\ref{lem:gradineq}, \ref{lem:tangency} and~\ref{lem:lipschitz}, and $K$ is chosen as the least positive integer satisfying the rational inequalities \eqref{eq:Kchoice}.

\emph{GAS.} The sandwich \eqref{eq:sandwich} gives $\beta_H<0\iff\beta_F<0$: if $\beta_F<0$, both entries of the upper bound are negative, and if $\beta_F\ge0$, the lower bound gives $\beta_H\ge0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:gascrit}, applied with the Euclidean form to $F$ and with $Q$ to $H$, proves \eqref{eq:mainGAS}.

\emph{Lyapunov stability.} By \eqref{eq:AHcone}, $kM_F(\tau)=\max_{p\in\Sigma}A_H(p,\tau)\le M_H(\tau)$ for all $\tau\ge0$, so $M_F^*\le M_H^*/k$. Conversely, let $y\in S_Q$ and $\tau\ge0$, and let $t_0=\inf\{t\ge0:\phi^H_t(y)\in\mathcal{T}\}\in[0,\infty]$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:tube}, $a_H(\phi^H_ty)<-1$ for $0\le t<t_0$. If $\tau\le t_0$, then $A_H(y,\tau)\le-\tau\le0$. If $\tau>t_0$, then $\phi^H_{t_0}(y)\in\mathcal{T}$ because $\mathcal{T}$ is closed, and Proposition~\ref{prop:shadow}, applied with the horizon $\tau-t_0$, gives $q=\sigma\nu_k(u)\in\Sigma$ with $A_H(\phi^H_{t_0}y,\tau-t_0)\le A_H(q,\tau-t_0)+C_*$. By the cocycle identity \eqref{eq:cocycleid} and \eqref{eq:AHcone},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mainest}
A_H(y,\tau)\le-t_0+k\,A_F(u,\tau-t_0)+C_*\qquad(\tau>t_0).
\end{equation}
Hence $M_F^*<\infty$ implies $M_H^*\le\max\{0,kM_F^*+C_*\}<\infty$. Thus $M_F^*<\infty$ if and only if $M_H^*<\infty$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:lyap}, applied with the Euclidean form to $F$ and with $Q$ to $H$, proves \eqref{eq:mainLS}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:padding}
Let $H:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m$ be homogeneous cubic, let $j\ge0$ and $N\ge m$. For $(x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^{N-m}$ define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hhat}
\widehat H(x,z)=\bigl(|x|^2+|z|^2\bigr)^j\bigl(H(x),-z_1^3,\dots,-z_{N-m}^3\bigr).
\end{equation}
Then $\widehat H$ is homogeneous of degree $3+2j$; its origin is GAS if and only if the origin of $H$ is GAS, and Lyapunov stable if and only if the origin of $H$ is Lyapunov stable.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $H_0(x,z)=(H(x),-z_1^3,\dots,-z_{N-m}^3)$. The system $\dot{(x,z)}=H_0(x,z)$ is the product of $\dot x=H(x)$ with the independent scalar equations $\dot z_i=-z_i^3$, whose solutions exist for all $t\ge0$, satisfy $|z_i(t)|\le|z_i(0)|$, and tend to $0$. Hence the origin of $H_0$ is GAS if and only if that of $H$ is; for the reverse implication, the invariant subspace $\{z=0\}$ reproduces every trajectory of $H$. In the same way, a bound $|x(t)|\le C|x(0)|$ for $H$ gives a bound for $H_0$ with respect to the norm $|x|+|z|$ and conversely, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling} the origin of $H_0$ is Lyapunov stable if and only if that of $H$ is. On the Euclidean unit sphere the factor $(|x|^2+|z|^2)^j$ equals one, so $\widehat H$ and $H_0$ have the same angular vector field and the same radial rate, and therefore the same quantities $\beta$ and $M^*$. Lemmas~\ref{lem:gascrit} and~\ref{lem:lyap} show that $\widehat H$ and $H_0$ have the same answer for GAS and for Lyapunov stability.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:even}
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be homogeneous of even degree $2k\ge2$, and define $\tilde f(x,w)=(w\,f(x),0)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$. Then $\tilde f$ is homogeneous of degree $2k+1$, and the origin is Lyapunov stable for $\tilde f$ if and only if it is Lyapunov stable for $f$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Along solutions of $\dot z=\tilde f(z)$, $z=(x,w)$, the coordinate $w(t)=w_0$ is constant and $\dot x=w_0f(x)$. Write $\phi^f$ for the flow of $f$. If $w_0\ge0$, then $x(t)=\phi^f(w_0t,x_0)$. If $w_0<0$, then $\zeta=-x$ satisfies $\dot\zeta=-w_0f(x)=|w_0|f(-\zeta)=|w_0|f(\zeta)$, because $f$ is even, so $x(t)=-\phi^f(|w_0|t,-x_0)$.

If $f$ is Lyapunov stable, Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling} gives $C\ge1$ such that $\phi^f(t,x)$ exists and $|\phi^f(t,x)|\le C|x|$ for all $t\ge0$. By the formulas above, every solution of $\dot z=\tilde f(z)$ is global and satisfies $|x(t)|+|w(t)|\le C(|x_0|+|w_0|)$, so $\tilde f$ is Lyapunov stable by Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling}. Conversely, if $\tilde f$ is Lyapunov stable with constant $C$ for the norm $|x|+|w|$, then for $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ the solution from $(x_0,\varepsilon)$ is global and $|\phi^f(\varepsilon t,x_0)|\le C(|x_0|+\varepsilon)$ for all $t\ge0$. Hence $\phi^f(s,x_0)$ exists for all $s\ge0$, and letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $|\phi^f(s,x_0)|\le C|x_0|$. Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling} shows that $f$ is Lyapunov stable.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:linear}
For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, the origin of $\dot x=Ax$ is Lyapunov stable if and only if there is a symmetric positive definite matrix $P$ with $A^TP+PA\preceq0$. Consequently Lyapunov stability of rational linear vector fields is decidable, uniformly in $n$. GAS of rational linear vector fields is decidable as well, uniformly in $n$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
If such $P$ exists, $x^TPx$ is nonincreasing along solutions, so $|x(t)|^2\le c\,|x(0)|^2$ with $c=\lambda_{\max}(P)/\lambda_{\min}(P)$. Conversely, if the origin is Lyapunov stable, then every eigenvalue of $A$ has nonpositive real part, and every eigenvalue $\lambda$ on the imaginary axis, of algebraic multiplicity $q$, satisfies $\operatorname{rank}(A-\lambda I)=n-q$ \cite[Chapter~4, Theorem~4.5, p.~134]{Khalil}; that is, the Jordan blocks of the eigenvalues on the imaginary axis have size one. By the real Jordan form \cite[Chapter~3, Theorem~3.4.1.5, p.~202]{HornJohnson} there is an invertible $T$ with $T^{-1}AT=\mathrm{diag}(A_-,A_0)$, where every eigenvalue of $A_-$ has negative real part and $A_0=SJS^{-1}$ with $J$ block diagonal with blocks $0$ and $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-\omega\\\omega&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, so that $J^T=-J$. Let $P_-$ be the positive definite solution of $A_-^TP_-+P_-A_-=-I$ \cite[Chapter~4, Theorem~4.6, p.~136]{Khalil}, and put $P=T^{-T}\mathrm{diag}(P_-,S^{-T}S^{-1})T^{-1}$. Then $A^TP+PA=T^{-T}\mathrm{diag}\bigl(-I,\,S^{-T}(J^T+J)S^{-1}\bigr)T^{-1}=T^{-T}\mathrm{diag}(-I,0)T^{-1}\preceq0$. For rational $A$, the sentence
\[
\exists P\ \ \Bigl(P=P^T\wedge\forall x\,\bigl(x\ne0\Rightarrow x^TPx>0\bigr)\wedge\forall x\ x^T(A^TP+PA)x\le0\Bigr)
\]
has rational data and is decidable by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski}. The origin of $\dot x=Ax$ is GAS if and only if every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part; writing $\det\bigl((\xi+i\zeta)I-A\bigr)=U(\xi,\zeta)+iV(\xi,\zeta)$ with $U,V\in\mathbb{Q}[\xi,\zeta]$ computable from $A$, this is the sentence $\forall\xi\,\forall\zeta\,\bigl(U=0\wedge V=0\Rightarrow\xi<0\bigr)$, which is decidable by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniform}
There is a single algorithm which, given $n\ge1$, $k\ge1$ and the rational coefficients of a homogeneous vector field $F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ of degree $2k+1$, outputs the rational coefficients of a homogeneous cubic vector field $H:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m$, $m=\binom{n+k-1}{k}$, satisfying \eqref{eq:mainGAS} and \eqref{eq:mainLS}.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Every step in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization} is computable from $(n,k,F)$: the index set $A_k$, the form $Q$, the list of binomials and $W$ depend only on $(n,k)$; $G$ is obtained by expanding $D\nu_k(x)F(x)$; the rationals $\eta,c,C_F,A_F,L_G$ are found by searches over rationals in which every step is a decision of a sentence by Theorem~\ref{thm:tarski}, and these searches terminate by Lemmas~\ref{lem:gradineq}, \ref{lem:tangency} and~\ref{lem:lipschitz}; and $K$ is the least positive integer satisfying \eqref{eq:Kchoice}. None of these steps depends on $(n,k)$ other than through finite data computed from it.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Throughout, invalid codes are sent to a fixed negative instance of the target problem: for a target of dimension $N$ and odd degree $e$ we use $x\mapsto|x|^{e-1}x$, which is neither GAS nor Lyapunov stable, since $\frac{d}{dt}|x|^2=2|x|^{e+1}>0$ for $x\ne0$ and nonzero solutions blow up in finite time. Let $c_\pm$ denote the codes of $x\mapsto\mp x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^1$; the origin is GAS and Lyapunov stable for $c_+$, and neither for $c_-$.

(i) Apply the map of Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization}.

(ii) Apply the computable map $H\mapsto\widehat H$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:padding}.

(iii) We show $\mathrm{HGAS}\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,3)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}$ for each fixed odd $d\ge3$; by transitivity this gives the assertion. For the first reduction, let $e$ code $(n,d',f)$. If $e$ is invalid, output $c_-$. If $d'$ is even, output $c_-$, by Remark~\ref{rem:even}. If $d'=1$, decide GAS by Lemma~\ref{lem:linear} and output $c_+$ or $c_-$. If $d'=2k+1\ge3$, output $\bigl(\binom{n+k-1}{k},H\bigr)$ with $H$ given by Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform}. This map is total and computable, and it is a many-one reduction by Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization}. For $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,3)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)$ with $d=3+2j$, send $(m,H)$ to $(m,\widehat H)$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:padding} with $N=m$. For $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}$, send $(n,f)$ to the code of $(n,d,f)$.

(iv) We show $\mathrm{HLS}\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HLS}(\cdot,3)$; the reductions $\mathrm{HLS}(\cdot,3)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HLS}(\cdot,d)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HLS}$ for odd $d\ge3$ are the same as in (iii), and $\mathrm{HLS}(\cdot,d)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HLS}$ holds for every $d$. Let $e$ code $(n,d',f)$. If $e$ is invalid, output $c_-$. If $d'=1$, decide Lyapunov stability by Lemma~\ref{lem:linear} and output $c_+$ or $c_-$. If $d'=2k$ is even, replace $(n,f)$ by $(n+1,\tilde f)$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:even}, which has degree $2k+1$ and the same answer. If the degree is now $2k+1$ and the dimension $n'$, output $\bigl(\binom{n'+k-1}{k},H\bigr)$ with $H$ given by Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:even} and Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization} this is a many-one reduction.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:transfer}
Let $n_0,k_0\ge1$ and $m_0=\binom{n_0+k_0-1}{k_0}$. If $\mathrm{HGAS}(n_0,2k_0+1)$ is undecidable (respectively many-one hard, respectively many-one complete), then so is $\mathrm{HGAS}(N,d)$ for every $N\ge m_0$ and every odd $d\ge3$. The same holds with $\mathrm{HLS}$ in place of $\mathrm{HGAS}$ for undecidability and for many-one hardness.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:normalform}(i) and (ii), $\mathrm{HGAS}(n_0,2k_0+1)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}(m_0,3)\le_{\mathrm m}\mathrm{HGAS}(N,d)$, and likewise for $\mathrm{HLS}$. Undecidability and many-one hardness pass from the source to the target of a many-one reduction by \ref{C:trans}. Membership of $\mathrm{HGAS}(N,d)$ in the class of r.e.\ sets is Proposition~\ref{prop:re}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The construction of \cite[Sections~3--6]{Korda} applies to any register machine $\mathsf U$ (see Section~\ref{subsec:computability}; this model is used because a step of such a machine changes one of finitely many natural numbers by $\pm1$, which is easy to imitate by a vector field) and produces, computably in $n$, a homogeneous vector field $F_n:\mathbb{R}^{N_K}\to\mathbb{R}^{N_K}$ with rational coefficients, of an odd degree $D_K=2k_K+1$ which does not depend on $n$, such that $\mathsf U$ halts on $n$ if and only if the origin is Lyapunov stable for $F_n$ \cite[(1.1) and Section~6]{Korda}. Take for $\mathsf U$ the machine of \cite[Remark~3.2]{Korda}, which is obtained from a universal Turing machine. The encoding of input words as numerals is a computable many-one reduction from the halting set of that Turing machine to the halting set of $\mathsf U$; the halting set of a universal Turing machine is many-one hard by the argument of \ref{C:K}, so the halting set of $\mathsf U$ is many-one hard by \ref{C:trans}. Hence $\mathrm{HLS}(N_K,D_K)$ is many-one hard, and Corollary~\ref{cor:transfer} shows that $\mathrm{HLS}(N,d)$ is many-one hard for every $N\ge m_0=\binom{N_K+k_K-1}{k_K}$ and every odd $d\ge3$. The remaining assertions follow from Section~\ref{subsec:computability}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:dim5}
Let $D_5=2k_5+1$ be the odd degree of \cite[Theorem~3.1]{KordaSupp}. By \cite[Theorem~5.1 and the proof of Theorem~3.1]{KordaSupp}, there is a computable map $n\mapsto F_n$ into rational homogeneous vector fields on $\mathbb{R}^5$ of degree $D_5$ such that the origin is Lyapunov stable for $F_n$ if and only if a fixed reversible two-counter machine $\mathsf V$ (a register machine with two registers whose steps can be undone uniquely \cite[Section~6]{KordaSupp}) does not halt from the configuration $(1,(2^n,0))$, and the set of $n$ for which $\mathsf V$ halts from this configuration is undecidable \cite[Theorem~6.2(a)]{KordaSupp}. Composing with Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization} and Lemma~\ref{lem:padding} shows that $\mathrm{HLS}(N,d)$ is undecidable for every $N\ge\binom{k_5+4}{4}$ and every odd $d\ge3$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:bothsides}
The two reductions run in opposite directions: in \cite{Korda} halting corresponds to stability, in \cite[Part~I]{KordaSupp} to instability. If the halting set in \cite[Theorem~6.2(a)]{KordaSupp} is many-one complete, as one expects from the universality of the machines on which it is based but which is not stated there, then the argument of Remark~\ref{rem:dim5} shows that every co-r.e.\ set (complement of an r.e.\ set) many-one reduces to $\mathrm{HLS}(N,d)$ for $N\ge\binom{k_5+4}{4}$ and odd $d\ge3$. For $N\ge\max\{m_0,\binom{k_5+4}{4}\}$ the set $\mathrm{HLS}(N,d)$ would then be neither r.e.\ nor co-r.e.: in contrast with GAS (Proposition~\ref{prop:re}), neither the stable nor the unstable cubic vector fields could be enumerated.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:gas-id}
There is $N'\ge1$ such that no algorithm decides, given a homogeneous cubic vector field $H:\mathbb{R}^{N'}\to\mathbb{R}^{N'}$ with rational coefficients, either of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem whether the origin is GAS for $\dot y=H(y)-y$;
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem whether every solution of $\dot y=H(y)$ exists for all $t\ge0$.
\end{enumerate}
Every instance $f=H-\mathrm{id}$ in (i) has linearization $Df(0)=-I$ at the origin, so the undecidable distinction concerns global behavior only.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
In the proof of \cite[Theorem~3.3]{KordaSupp} a computable map $n\mapsto F_n$ is constructed, into rational homogeneous vector fields on a fixed $\mathbb{R}^{N''}$ of a fixed odd degree $2k''+1$, such that the following holds for a fixed register machine $\mathsf U$ with undecidable halting problem. If $\mathsf U$ halts on $n$, then every solution of $\dot Y=F_n(Y)$ is global and satisfies $|Y(t)|\le e^{B_n}|Y(0)|$ for some $B_n$ \cite[Theorem~12.5(H) and Proposition~12.3(a)]{KordaSupp}; if $\mathsf U$ does not halt on $n$, then some solution of $\dot Y=F_n(Y)$ blows up in finite time \cite[Theorem~12.5(N) and Proposition~12.3(b)]{KordaSupp}. Let $H_n$ be the cubic vector field produced from $F_n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization}, on $\mathbb{R}^{N'}$ with $N'=\binom{N''+k''-1}{k''}$.

If $\mathsf U$ halts on $n$, then $F_n$ is Lyapunov stable by Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling}, hence so is $H_n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:cubicization}, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:scaling} again every solution of $\dot y=H_n(y)$ is global and satisfies $|y(t)|\le C|y(0)|$ for some $C$. In particular $\dot y=H_n(y)$ is forward complete, and by \cite[Lemma~12.1(b)]{KordaSupp} every solution of $\dot z=H_n(z)-z$ satisfies $|z(t)|\le Ce^{-t}|z(0)|$, so the origin is GAS.

If $\mathsf U$ does not halt on $n$, let $x$ be a solution of $\dot x=F_n(x)$ which blows up at a finite time $t_*$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:conedyn}(b), $y=\nu_{k''}(x)$ solves $\dot y=H_n(y)$ on $[0,t_*)$, and $\|y(t)\|_Q=|x(t)|^{k''}$ is unbounded there. Thus $\dot y=H_n(y)$ is not forward complete, and by \cite[Lemma~12.1(c)]{KordaSupp} some solution of $\dot z=H_n(z)-z$ blows up in finite time, so the origin is not GAS.

An algorithm for (i) or (ii) would therefore decide the halting problem of $\mathsf U$. Finally, $D(H-\mathrm{id})(0)=-I$ because $H$ is cubic.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:mrdp}
For every r.e.\ set $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ there are $k\ge1$ and a polynomial $P\in\mathbb{Z}[t,y_1,\dots,y_k]$ such that for every $e\in\mathbb{N}$, $e\in S$ if and only if $P(e,y)=0$ for some $y\in\mathbb{N}^k$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:template}
There are integers $q,r\ge1$, matrices $A_*,B_*\in\mathbb{Z}^{r\times q}$ and vectors $c_0,c_1\in\mathbb{Z}^r$ such that every column of $B_*$ is nonzero and, with $c(e)=c_0+e\,c_1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:template}
e\in K\iff\exists n\in\mathbb{Z}^q:\ A_*n^{\circ2}+B_*n=c(e)\qquad(e\in\mathbb{N}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:mrdp} to $S=K$ and fix the resulting polynomial $P(t,y)$. Write $P=P^+-P^-$, where $P^\pm$ have nonnegative coefficients, and fix two finite lists of instructions which compute $P^+(t,y)+1$ and $P^-(t,y)+1$, respectively, where each instruction produces either the constant $1$ or the sum or the product of two inputs or earlier results. Introduce an integer variable for $t$, for each $y_i$, and for the output of each instruction, and write down the following equations: $t=e$; $g=1$ for each instruction producing the constant $1$; $g=g'+g''$ for each addition; and for each multiplication $g=g'g''$ a new variable $w$ with the two equations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:polarization}
w=g'+g'',\qquad w^2-g'^2-g''^2-2g=0;
\end{equation}
finally, the equation equating the two outputs, and, for each $i$, four new variables $a_{i1},\dots,a_{i4}$ and the equation $y_i=a_{i1}^2+a_{i2}^2+a_{i3}^2+a_{i4}^2$. Every equation is an integer linear combination of the variables and their squares, and only the right-hand side of the equation $t=e$ depends on $e$, affinely. Thus the system has the form \eqref{eq:dql} with fixed $A,B$ and right-hand side $c_0+ec_1$.

If $P(e,y)=0$ with $y\in\mathbb{N}^k$, assign to every variable its value in the computation, choose the $a_{i\cdot}$ by Lagrange's four-square theorem \cite[Chapter~XX, Theorem~369, p.~399]{HardyWright} (and $a_{i\cdot}=0$ if $y_i=0$), and put $w=g'+g''$; this solves the system. Conversely, in an integer solution every $y_i$ is a sum of four squares, hence in $\mathbb{N}$; the two equations \eqref{eq:polarization} give $2g=(g'+g'')^2-g'^2-g''^2=2g'g''$, so every instruction is computed correctly, and $P^+(e,y)+1=P^-(e,y)+1$. Hence the system is solvable if and only if $e\in K$.

Finally, to make every column of $B$ nonzero, add for every variable $x_j$ a duplicate variable $x_j'$ and the equation $x_j-x_j'=0$, leaving the old equations unchanged. If $x$ solves the old system, $(x,x)$ solves the new one, and conversely the first half of a solution of the new system solves the old one. In the new equation for $x_j$ the column of $x_j$ has entry $+1$ and that of $x_j'$ has entry $-1$, so every column of the new linear coefficient matrix is nonzero. The new system still has the form \eqref{eq:template}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:constterm}
The Fourier series of $\mathfrak D_e$ converges absolutely, and its constant term is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:constterm}
\frac1{(2\pi)^{q+r}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{q+r}}\mathfrak D_e(\varphi)\,d\varphi=\sum_{\substack{n\in\mathbb{Z}^q\\An^{\circ2}+Bn=c(e)}}(\lambda\eta)^{|n|^2}.
\end{equation}
In particular the constant term is a positive real number if $e\in K$, and it is zero if $e\notin K$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Expanding the $j$-th factor gives $\sum_{n_j,s_j\in\mathbb{Z}}\lambda^{n_j^2}\eta^{|s_j|}Q_j^{n_j^2-s_j}V_j^{n_j}S_j^{s_j}$, a series of characters with absolutely summable coefficients; hence the finite product converges absolutely, and it may be integrated term by term. The character $Q_j^{n_j^2-s_j}$ involves only $\varphi_j$, so a term survives integration over the private phases only if $s_j=n_j^2$ for all $j$. The remaining character is $\prod_l\chi_l^{\sum_j(A_{lj}n_j^2+B_{lj}n_j)-c_l(e)}$, which survives integration over the equation phases only if $An^{\circ2}+Bn=c(e)$. The surviving terms are $\prod_j\lambda^{n_j^2}\eta^{n_j^2}=(\lambda\eta)^{|n|^2}$. They are positive, so there is no cancellation, and the sum is nonempty exactly when \eqref{eq:template} has a solution, that is, when $e\in K$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:template}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
For the single equation $n^2+n=2$, with one private phase and one equation phase, the detector is
\[
\chi^{-2}\Theta_\lambda(Q,\chi)P_\eta(Q^{-1}\chi)=\sum_{n,s\in\mathbb{Z}}\lambda^{n^2}\eta^{|s|}Q^{n^2-s}\chi^{n+s-2}.
\]
Integration over the private phase keeps only the terms with $s=n^2$, and integration over the equation phase then keeps only those with $n^2+n=2$. The two solutions $n=1$ and $n=-2$ contribute $(\lambda\eta)+(\lambda\eta)^4>0$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:controller}
The functions $r_\ell^2+s_\ell^2$ and $|\zeta_\ell|^2$ are constant along solutions of \eqref{eq:controller}. Let $(r_\ell(t),s_\ell(t))$ be a solution with $r_\ell^2+s_\ell^2=1$ which is forward recurrent, that is, which returns arbitrarily close to $(r_\ell(0),s_\ell(0))$ at arbitrarily large times. Then it is one of the four equilibria $r_\ell=\epsilon_\ell p_\ell^{-1/2}$, $s_\ell=\pm(1-p_\ell^{-1})^{1/2}$, $\epsilon_\ell\in\{-1,1\}$, and then $\omega_\ell=\epsilon_\ell\sqrt{p_\ell}$ and $\zeta_\ell(t)=\zeta_\ell(0)e^{i\omega_\ell t}$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The first two components of \eqref{eq:controller} are $(p_\ell r_\ell^2-1)$ times the rotation vector field $(-s_\ell,r_\ell)$, so $r_\ell^2+s_\ell^2$ is constant; and $\frac d{dt}|\zeta_\ell|^2=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar\zeta_\ell\dot\zeta_\ell)=0$. On the unit circle write $(r_\ell,s_\ell)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$; then $\dot\theta=p_\ell\cos^2\theta-1$. Since $p_\ell\ge2$, the right side has exactly four zeros on the circle, and on each open arc between consecutive zeros it has a constant sign. A solution starting on such an arc is therefore strictly monotone in $\theta$ and converges to an endpoint of the arc, so it does not return near its initial point. Hence a forward recurrent solution is an equilibrium, $p_\ell r_\ell^2=1$, and the last assertion follows from $\dot\zeta_\ell=i\omega_\ell\zeta_\ell$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:radicals}
Let $p_1,\dots,p_d$ be distinct primes, $P=\max_ap_a$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^d$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}^d\setminus\{0\}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smalldiv}
\Bigl|\sum_{a=1}^dk_a\epsilon_a\sqrt{p_a}\Bigr|\ge\bigl(\sqrt P\,|k|_1\bigr)^{1-2^d}>0,\qquad|k|_1=\sum_a|k_a|.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:radicals} in Appendix~\ref{app:radicals}, the numbers $\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_d}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, so $L(\delta):=\sum_ak_a\delta_a\sqrt{p_a}\ne0$ for every $\delta\in\{-1,1\}^d$. Consider $\Pi=\prod_{\delta\in\{-1,1\}^d}L(\delta)$ as a polynomial with integer coefficients in the indeterminates $u_a$, after replacing $\sqrt{p_a}$ by $u_a$. Changing the sign of one $u_a$ permutes the factors, so $\Pi$ is unchanged; hence every monomial of $\Pi$ has even degree in every $u_a$, and $\Pi$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients in $u_a^2=p_a$. Thus $\Pi$ is a nonzero integer, and $|\Pi|\ge1$. Every factor satisfies $|L(\delta)|\le\sqrt P|k|_1$, and \eqref{eq:smalldiv} follows by dividing $|\Pi|\ge1$ by the $2^d-1$ factors with $\delta\ne\epsilon$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:irrational}
For every $j$, $\Omega_j\ne0$ and $N_j/\Omega_j\notin\mathbb{Q}$. Moreover $k\cdot\omega\ne0$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}^{q+r}\setminus\{0\}$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The last assertion is Lemma~\ref{lem:radicals}, and $\Omega_j=4\epsilon_j\sqrt{p_j}\ne0$. If $N_j/\Omega_j=a/b$ with integers $a,b$, $b\ne0$, then $bN_j-a\Omega_j=k\cdot\omega$ with $k_j=-4a$, $k_{q+l}=4bB_{lj}$, and all other entries zero. By Lemma~\ref{lem:radicals} this $k$ is zero; so $a=0$, and then $bB_j=0$ with $B_j\ne0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:template}) gives $b=0$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:avg}
Let $g$ have an absolutely convergent Fourier series on $\mathbb{T}^d$, let $\varphi_0\in\mathbb{T}^d$, and let $\omega\in\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfy $k\cdot\omega\ne0$ whenever $\hat g_k\ne0$ and $k\ne0$. Then $\frac1T\int_0^Tg(\varphi_0+\omega t)\,dt\to\hat g_0$ as $T\to\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
For each $k$ the average of $\hat g_ke^{ik\cdot(\varphi_0+\omega t)}$ over $[0,T]$ is $\hat g_k$ if $k=0$, and is bounded by $2|\hat g_k|/(T|k\cdot\omega|)\to0$ otherwise. Since the averages of the individual terms are bounded by $|\hat g_k|$, which is summable, dominated convergence for series gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:thetagamma}
For every $\gamma\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ there is a $3\times3$ matrix $\sigma_\gamma$, with exactly one entry $\pm1$ in every row and every column and zeros elsewhere, such that
\[
(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_3^4,\vartheta_4^4)^T(\gamma\tau)=j(\gamma,\tau)^2\,\sigma_\gamma\,(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_3^4,\vartheta_4^4)^T(\tau)\qquad(\tau\in\mathbb{H}).
\]
Consequently the function $m(\tau)=\operatorname{Im}(\tau)\max_{k=2,3,4}|\vartheta_k(\tau)|^4$ satisfies $m(\gamma\tau)=m(\tau)$ for $\gamma\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:modcanon}
The map $\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}=(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_4^4,E_2,\vartheta_3)$ satisfies $D\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}})$ and $Y^4=A+C$ on $\mathbb{H}$. Consequently, for every $\tau_0\in\mathbb{H}$, $t\mapsto\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}(\tau_0+\Omega t/\pi)$ solves \eqref{eq:modblock}.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
By \ref{th:ode} and \ref{th:jacobi}, $D\vartheta_2^4=4\vartheta_2^4D\log\vartheta_2=\frac13\vartheta_2^4(E_2+\vartheta_2^4+2\vartheta_4^4)$, and similarly for the other components; for $\mathcal{D}_E$ use $\vartheta_2^8+\vartheta_3^8+\vartheta_4^8=2(\vartheta_2^8+\vartheta_2^4\vartheta_4^4+\vartheta_4^8)$, which follows from \ref{th:jacobi}. The identity $Y^4=A+C$ is \ref{th:jacobi}. For the last assertion note $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}(\tau_0+\Omega t/\pi)=\frac\Omega\pi\cdot\pi i\,D\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:modgeneral}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem Let $M\in SL_2(\mathbb{C})$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be open with $M(U)\subseteq\mathbb{H}$, write $j(\tau)=j(M,\tau)$, and let $\rho$ be holomorphic on $U$ with $\rho^4=j^{-2}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:modfamily}
\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\tau)=\Bigl(\frac{\vartheta_2^4(M\tau)}{j(\tau)^2},\ \frac{\vartheta_4^4(M\tau)}{j(\tau)^2},\ \frac{E_2(M\tau)}{j(\tau)^2}+\frac{6ic}{\pi j(\tau)},\ \rho(\tau)\vartheta_3(M\tau)\Bigr),
\end{equation}
where $c$ is the lower left entry of $M$, satisfies $D\mathbf m_{M,\rho}=\mathcal{D}(\mathbf m_{M,\rho})$ and $Y^4=A+C$ on $U$.
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem Let $\mathbf m^*=(A^*,C^*,E^*,Y^*)$ satisfy $Y^{*4}=A^*+C^*$ and $A^*C^*(A^*+C^*)\ne0$, let $\tau^*\in\mathbb{C}$, and let $T^*\in\mathbb{H}$ with $\Lambda(T^*)=A^*/(A^*+C^*)$. Then there are $M,U,\rho$ as in (a), with $\tau^*\in U$, such that $M\tau^*=T^*$ and $\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\tau^*)=\mathbf m^*$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
(a) Write $T=M\tau$, so $dT/d\tau=j^{-2}$ and $dj/d\tau=c$, and let $\vartheta_k,E_2$ denote values at $T$. Then $D_\tau A=(\pi i)^{-1}\frac{d}{d\tau}(\vartheta_2^4j^{-2})=j^{-4}(D\vartheta_2^4)+\frac{2ic}\pi j^{-3}\vartheta_2^4$, while by Lemma~\ref{lem:modcanon}
\[
\mathcal{D}_A(\mathbf m_{M,\rho})=\tfrac13\vartheta_2^4j^{-2}\Bigl(\frac{E_2+\vartheta_2^4+2\vartheta_4^4}{j^2}+\frac{6ic}{\pi j}\Bigr)=j^{-4}(D\vartheta_2^4)+\frac{2ic}{\pi}j^{-3}\vartheta_2^4.
\]
The components $C$, $E$ and $Y$ are checked in the same way, using $\rho'/\rho=-c/(2j)$ for $Y$. The identity $Y^4=A+C$ follows from \ref{th:jacobi}.

(b) Put $v^*=(A^*+C^*)/\vartheta_3^4(T^*)\ne0$ and choose $j^*$ with $(j^*)^{-2}=v^*$. Define $c=\pi j^*(E^*-v^*E_2(T^*))/(6i)$, $d=j^*-c\tau^*$, $a=(1+cT^*j^*)/j^*$ and $b=T^*j^*-a\tau^*$. Then $ad-bc=1$, $c\tau^*+d=j^*$ and $a\tau^*+b=T^*j^*$, so $M=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ satisfies $M\tau^*=T^*$ and $j(M,\tau^*)=j^*$. By continuity there is a disc $U\ni\tau^*$ with $M(U)\subseteq\mathbb{H}$ and $j(M,\cdot)\ne0$ on $U$; let $\rho$ be the holomorphic fourth root of $j(M,\cdot)^{-2}$ on the disc $U$ with $\rho(\tau^*)=Y^*/\vartheta_3(T^*)$, which exists since $j(M,\cdot)$ has no zero on $U$ and $(Y^*/\vartheta_3(T^*))^4=v^*=(j^*)^{-2}$. Now $A=v^*\vartheta_2^4(T^*)=(A^*+C^*)\Lambda(T^*)=A^*$, $C=v^*\vartheta_4^4(T^*)=(A^*+C^*)(1-\Lambda(T^*))=C^*$ by \ref{th:jacobi}, $E=v^*E_2(T^*)+6ic/(\pi j^*)=E^*$, and $Y=Y^*$ at $\tau^*$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:moddiv}
Each of the sets $\{A=0\}$, $\{C=0\}$, $\{A+C=0\}$ is invariant under \eqref{eq:modblock}. If $\mathbf m:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}^4$ is a solution of \eqref{eq:modblock} on $\{Y^4=A+C\}$ with $A(0)C(0)(A(0)+C(0))=0$ which is forward recurrent, then $\mathbf m$ is constant.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We have $\mathcal{D}_A=A\cdot\frac13(E+A+2C)$, $\mathcal{D}_C=C\cdot\frac13(E-2A-C)$ and $\mathcal{D}_A+\mathcal{D}_C=(A+C)\cdot\frac13(E+A-C)$, so each of $A$, $C$ and $A+C$ is a solution of a scalar linear equation along a solution of \eqref{eq:modblock}, and either vanishes identically or never. On $\{A=0\}$ the function $u=E-C$ satisfies $\dot u=\frac{i\Omega}6u^2$; on $\{C=0\}$ the function $u=E+A$ satisfies the same equation; on $\{A+C=0\}$ we have $Y=0$, $C=-A$, and $u=E-A$ satisfies the same equation. A solution of $\dot u=\frac{i\Omega}6u^2$ defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$ is $u(t)=u(0)/(1-i\Omega u(0)t/6)$, and if $u(0)\ne0$ then $u(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, so $\mathbf m$ is not forward recurrent. Hence $u\equiv0$, and then \eqref{eq:modsys} shows that $\dot{\mathbf m}=0$ in each of the three cases.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:modcomplete}
Let $\mathbf m:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}^4$ be a solution of \eqref{eq:modblock} with $Y^4=A+C$ and $A(0)C(0)(A(0)+C(0))\ne0$. Then there is $M\in SL_2(\mathbb{C})$ with $M(\mathbb{R})\subseteq\mathbb{H}$ such that, for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbf m(t)=\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\Omega t/\pi)$ with $\rho(\Omega t/\pi)=Y(t)/\vartheta_3(M(\Omega t/\pi))$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:moddiv}, $A$, $C$ and $A+C$ never vanish, so $\ell(t)=A(t)/(A(t)+C(t))$ is a continuous path in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}$. By \ref{th:lambda} and the lifting criterion for covering maps \cite[Proposition~1.33, p.~61]{Hatcher}, which applies since $\mathbb{R}$ is simply connected and locally path-connected, there is a continuous $T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{H}$ with $\Lambda\circ T=\ell$. Fix $t^*\in\mathbb{R}$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:modgeneral}(b) with $\tau^*=\Omega t^*/\pi$, $\mathbf m^*=\mathbf m(t^*)$ and $T^*=T(t^*)$; this gives $(M_{t^*},\rho_{t^*})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:modgeneral}(a), $t\mapsto\mathbf m_{M_{t^*},\rho_{t^*}}(\Omega t/\pi)$ solves \eqref{eq:modblock} near $t^*$, and it agrees with $\mathbf m$ at $t^*$; by uniqueness the two agree near $t^*$. Hence $\Lambda(M_{t^*}(\Omega t/\pi))=\ell(t)$ near $t^*$, so $t\mapsto M_{t^*}(\Omega t/\pi)$ and $T$ are continuous lifts of $\ell$ which agree at $t^*$, and therefore agree near $t^*$ by uniqueness of lifts \cite[Proposition~1.34, p.~62]{Hatcher}. Two Möbius maps which agree on an interval are equal as maps (their matrices agree up to sign), so $t^*\mapsto M_{t^*}$, as a Möbius map, is locally constant; since $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, all $M_{t^*}$ define one Möbius map $M$, and $T(t)=M(\Omega t/\pi)$ for all $t$. The components $A,C,E$ of \eqref{eq:modfamily} do not change if the matrix of $M$ is replaced by its negative, and $\rho(\Omega t/\pi):=Y(t)/\vartheta_3(T(t))$ is continuous by \ref{th:nozero}, with $\rho^4=j(M,\cdot)^{-2}$ along $\Omega t/\pi$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:modshape}
Let $M\in SL_2(\mathbb{C})$ with $M(\mathbb{R})\subseteq\mathbb{H}$. Then exactly one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem $M(\infty)\in\mathbb{H}$. Then $\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\tau)\to0$ as $\tau\to\pm\infty$ in $\mathbb{R}$, for every continuous $\rho$ with $\rho^4=j(M,\cdot)^{-2}$.
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem There are $g\in SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $s\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ with $M\tau=g(i+s\tau)$ for all $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$; then $M(\infty)=g(\infty)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$.
\end{enumerate}
In case (b), put $u_x=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $h_\tau=g\,u_{s\tau}\in SL_2(\mathbb{R})$. Then $M\tau=h_\tau i$, and the components of $\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\tau)$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:modframe}
A=s\,\frac{\vartheta_2^4(h_\tau i)}{j(h_\tau,i)^2},\qquad C=s\,\frac{\vartheta_4^4(h_\tau i)}{j(h_\tau,i)^2},\qquad\max\{|A|,|C|,|A+C|\}=|s|\,m(h_\tau i).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
(a) Here the lower left entry $c$ of $M$ is nonzero, since otherwise $M(\infty)=\infty$. As $\tau\to\pm\infty$, $M\tau\to M(\infty)\in\mathbb{H}$, so the theta constants and $E_2$ at $M\tau$ stay bounded, while $|j(M,\tau)|\to\infty$; hence every component of \eqref{eq:modfamily} tends to zero.

(b) If $M(\infty)\notin\mathbb{H}$, then $x^*=M(\infty)$, a limit of points of $M(\mathbb{R})\subseteq\mathbb{H}$, lies in $\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$. Choose $g_0\in SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ with $g_0(\infty)=x^*$. Then $N=g_0^{-1}M$ fixes $\infty$, so $N\tau=\kappa\tau+b$ with $\kappa\ne0$, and $N(\mathbb{R})=g_0^{-1}(M(\mathbb{R}))\subseteq\mathbb{H}$. A line $\{\kappa\tau+b:\tau\in\mathbb{R}\}$ lies in $\mathbb{H}$ only if $\kappa\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\operatorname{Im} b>0$. Writing $b=x_1+iy_1$ and $h_1=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sqrt{y_1}&x_1/\sqrt{y_1}\\0&1/\sqrt{y_1}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, we get $N\tau=h_1(i+s\tau)$ with $s=\kappa/y_1$, and $g=g_0h_1$ works.

For \eqref{eq:modframe}, $M$ is the composition of $g$ with $\tau\mapsto i+s\tau$, whose matrix is $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}s^{1/2}&is^{-1/2}\\0&s^{-1/2}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ for a choice of $s^{1/2}\in\mathbb{C}$. Hence, if $g=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, then $j(M,\tau)=s^{-1/2}(c(i+s\tau)+d)=s^{-1/2}j(h_\tau,i)$, because $h_\tau$ has lower row $(c,cs\tau+d)$. This gives the formulas for $A$ and $C$, and $A+C=Y^4=s\vartheta_3^4(h_\tau i)/j(h_\tau,i)^2$. Since $|j(h_\tau,i)|^{-2}=\operatorname{Im}(h_\tau i)$, the last identity follows.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:modselect}
Let $\Omega\ne0$, let $\alpha(t)=\alpha_0+\Omega t$ with $\alpha_0\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\mathbf m:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}^4$ be a solution of \eqref{eq:modblock} with $Y^4=A+C$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem $\mathbf m$ is forward recurrent;
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem $\frac1T\int_0^T|\mathbf m(t)|^\mu\,dt$ is bounded for $T\ge1$, for some $\mu\ge1$;
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem $\langle Y\rangle=1$ and $\langle Y e^{-i\alpha}\rangle=2\lambda$.
\end{enumerate}
Put $\tau(t)=\tau_\lambda+\alpha(t)/\pi$. Then for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:modselect}
\mathbf m(t)=\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}(\tau(t)),\quad\text{that is,}\quad(A,C,E,Y)(t)=(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_4^4,E_2,\vartheta_3)(\tau(t)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1.} If $A(0)C(0)(A(0)+C(0))=0$, then $\mathbf m$ is constant by Lemma~\ref{lem:moddiv}, and $\langle Ye^{-i\alpha}\rangle=Y\langle e^{-i\alpha}\rangle=0\ne2\lambda$. Hence Proposition~\ref{prop:modcomplete} applies and gives $M$ with $\mathbf m(t)=\mathbf m_{M,\rho}(\Omega t/\pi)$. In case (a) of Lemma~\ref{lem:modshape}, $\mathbf m(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$ while $\mathbf m(0)\ne0$, contradicting (i). So we are in case (b), with $g\in SL_2(\mathbb{R})$, $s\ne0$, and base point $x^*=g(\infty)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$.

\emph{Step 2: $x^*$ is rational or $\infty$.} Suppose not. Let $X=\Gamma(2)\backslash SL_2(\mathbb{R})$, with the Haar probability measure $m_X$ and the horocycle flow $h(r)x=x\,u_{-r}$ ($r\in\mathbb{R}$, $x\in X$) of \cite[Chapter~11, \S11.5, p.~378]{EW}; the matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-r\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ used there is $u_{-r}$. Since $\Gamma(2)$ is a lattice in $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ by \ref{th:lambda}, the theorem of Dani and Smillie \cite{DaniSmillie}, in the form \cite[Chapter~11, Theorem~11.35, p.~399]{EW} (see also \cite{HubbardMiller}), gives: if $x\in X$ is not periodic, that is, $h(r)x\ne x$ for all $r>0$, then $\frac1T\int_0^T\psi(h(r)x)\,dr\to\int\psi\,dm_X$ as $T\to\infty$, for every compactly supported continuous $\psi$ on $X$. Let $J=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$. The map $\Phi:X\to X$, $\Phi(\Gamma(2)h)=\Gamma(2)JhJ^{-1}$, is well defined because $J\Gamma(2)J^{-1}=\Gamma(2)$; moreover $\Phi\circ\Phi$ is the identity, and $\Phi(x\,u_r)=\Phi(x)\,u_{-r}$ because $Ju_rJ^{-1}=u_{-r}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:modshape}, the points $g_t=g\,u_{s\Omega t/\pi}$ satisfy $|s|\,m(g_ti)\le2|\mathbf m(t)|$. Put $\nu=|s\Omega|/\pi>0$, put $g'=g$ if $s\Omega<0$ and $g'=JgJ^{-1}$ if $s\Omega>0$, and let $x_0=\Gamma(2)g'$. Then $\Gamma(2)g_t=h(\nu t)x_0$ if $s\Omega<0$, and $\Gamma(2)g_t=\Phi(h(\nu t)x_0)$ if $s\Omega>0$. The point $x_0$ is not periodic: otherwise $\gamma g'=g'u_{-r}$ for some $\gamma\in\Gamma(2)$ and $r>0$, so $\gamma=g'u_{-r}g'^{-1}\ne\pm I$ is parabolic with fixed point $g'(\infty)$, which is $x^*$ or $-x^*$ and hence irrational, but the fixed point of a parabolic $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is $\infty$ or $(a-d)/(2c)\in\mathbb{Q}$. The function $f(h)=m(hi)^\mu$ is continuous and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:thetagamma}, invariant under $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ on the left, so it defines a continuous function on $X$. It satisfies $f\circ\Phi=f$, because $JhJ^{-1}i=-\overline{hi}$ and $|\vartheta_k(-\bar\tau)|=|\vartheta_k(\tau)|$; hence $f(g_t)=f(h(\nu t)x_0)$ in both cases. Choose compactly supported continuous $0\le\psi_n\le f$ increasing to $f$. Then for every $n$, after the change of variables $r=\nu t$,
\[
\Bigl(\frac2{|s|}\Bigr)^\mu\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T|\mathbf m(t)|^\mu\,dt\ge\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^Tf(h(\nu t)x_0)\,dt\ge\int\psi_n\,dm_X,
\]
and $\int\psi_n\,dm_X\to\int f\,dm_X$. We claim that $\int f\,dm_X=\infty$, which contradicts (ii). Since $-I\in\Gamma(2)$, $X$ is also the quotient of $PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ by $\bar\Gamma(2)$; let $\pi$ be the quotient map. In the coordinates $hi=x+iy$ and the angle $\theta$ of the unit tangent vector, Haar measure on $PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ is $dx\,dy\,d\theta/y^2$, and $m_X(\pi(B))$ is a constant multiple of $\int_Bdx\,dy\,d\theta/y^2$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ on which $\pi$ is injective \cite[Chapter~9, Lemma~9.16, p.~306, and Propositions~9.19 and~9.20, pp.~311--313; Chapter~11, p.~357]{EW}. Let $\mathcal C=\{x+iy:|x|<1,\ y>2\}$. Then $\pi$ is injective on $\{h:hi\in\mathcal C\}$: if $\gamma\in\Gamma(2)$ has lower left entry $c\ne0$, then $|c|\ge2$ and $\operatorname{Im}(\gamma\tau)\le1/(c^2\operatorname{Im}\tau)<2$ for $\tau\in\mathcal C$, while the elements with $c=0$ are $\pm u_{2k}$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and $u_{2k}(\mathcal C)$ meets $\mathcal C$ only for $k=0$. On $\mathcal C$ we have $|\vartheta_3(\tau)-1|\le2\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-2\pi n^2}<\frac1{10}$, so $f\ge(y/2)^\mu$, and $\int_2^\infty y^{\mu-2}dy=\infty$ for $\mu\ge1$.

\emph{Step 3: the case $x^*\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$.} Now $x^*\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$, so there is $\gamma\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ with $\gamma(x^*)=\infty$. Then $\tilde M=\gamma M$ fixes $\infty$ and $\tilde M(\mathbb{R})\subseteq\mathbb{H}$, so, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:modshape}, $\tilde M\tau=\kappa\tau+b$ with $\kappa\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{Im} b>0$. Put $\tilde T(t)=\tilde M(\Omega t/\pi)=\kappa\Omega t/\pi+b$. The matrix of $\tilde M$ is $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\kappa^{1/2}&b\kappa^{-1/2}\\0&\kappa^{-1/2}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, so $j(M,\tau)=\pm\kappa^{-1/2}j(\gamma^{-1},\tilde M\tau)$, and the lower left entry of $M$ is $\pm\kappa^{1/2}c'$, where $c'$ is that of $\gamma^{-1}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:thetagamma} and \ref{th:E2} applied to $\gamma^{-1}$ then turn \eqref{eq:modfamily} into
\[
(A,C,A+C)(t)=\kappa\,(\Xi_2,\Xi_4,\Xi_3)(\tilde T(t)),\qquad E(t)=\kappa E_2(\tilde T(t)),
\]
where $(\Xi_2,\Xi_3,\Xi_4)^T=\sigma_{\gamma^{-1}}(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_3^4,\vartheta_4^4)^T$; here the terms of $E$ involving $c'$ cancel, and $\Xi_3=\Xi_2+\Xi_4$ by \ref{th:jacobi} at the points $\gamma^{-1}\tilde T(t)$. Since $\sigma_{\gamma^{-1}}$ is a signed permutation, $\Xi_3=\epsilon\vartheta_y^4$ for some $y\in\{2,3,4\}$ and $\epsilon=\pm1$. As $Y^4=A+C$, the continuous function $Y(t)/\vartheta_y(\tilde T(t))$ has constant fourth power $\epsilon\kappa$, so it is a constant $\tilde\rho$, and $Y(t)=\tilde\rho\,\vartheta_y(\tilde T(t))$.

Write $e^{\pi i\tilde T(t)}=e^{\pi ib}e^{i\kappa\Omega t}$, with $|e^{\pi ib}|<1$. The series for $\vartheta_y(\tilde T(t))$ converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, so averages may be taken term by term. If $y=2$, every term $e^{\pi i(n+1/2)^2\tilde T(t)}$ has nonzero frequency $(n+\frac12)^2\kappa\Omega$, so $\langle Y\rangle=0$, contradicting (iii). Hence $y\in\{3,4\}$, $Y(t)=\tilde\rho\bigl(1+2\sum_{n\ge1}(\pm1)^ne^{\pi in^2b}e^{in^2\kappa\Omega t}\bigr)$ with the sign $+$ for $y=3$ and $-$ for $y=4$, and $\langle Y\rangle=\tilde\rho$. Thus $\tilde\rho=1$ and $\epsilon\kappa=1$, so $\kappa=\pm1$. Next, $Y(t)e^{-i\alpha(t)}$ has the terms $e^{-i\alpha_0}e^{-i\Omega t}$ and $2(\pm1)^ne^{\pi in^2b}e^{-i\alpha_0}e^{i(n^2\kappa-1)\Omega t}$, $n\ge1$, and only frequencies zero survive averaging. Since $\langle Ye^{-i\alpha}\rangle=2\lambda\ne0$, some $n\ge1$ has $n^2\kappa=1$; so $\kappa=1$, $n=1$, and $2(\pm1)e^{\pi ib}e^{-i\alpha_0}=2\lambda$. Hence $|e^{\pi ib}|=\lambda$, that is $\operatorname{Im} b=\operatorname{Im}\tau_\lambda$, and $e^{\pi i\tilde T(t)}=\pm\lambda e^{i\alpha(t)}=\pm e^{\pi i\tau(t)}$. Thus $\tilde T(t)-\tau(t)$ is a constant integer, even if $y=3$ and odd if $y=4$. In both cases $\vartheta_y(\tilde T(t))=\vartheta_3(\tau(t))$ and $E_2(\tilde T(t))=E_2(\tau(t))$, because $\vartheta_3(\tau+2)=\vartheta_3(\tau)$, $\vartheta_4(\tau+1)=\vartheta_3(\tau)$ and $E_2(\tau+1)=E_2(\tau)$. By \ref{th:transf}, $\Xi_2(\tilde T(t))$ and $\Xi_4(\tilde T(t))$ are, in some order, $\epsilon_2\vartheta_2^4(\tau(t))$ and $\epsilon_4\vartheta_4^4(\tau(t))$ with $\epsilon_2,\epsilon_4\in\{\pm1\}$. Since $A+C=Y^4=\vartheta_2^4(\tau)+\vartheta_4^4(\tau)$, we get $(\epsilon_2-1)\vartheta_2^4(\tau(t))=(1-\epsilon_4)\vartheta_4^4(\tau(t))$; the left side has average zero (all its frequencies are nonzero) and the right side has average $1-\epsilon_4$, so $\epsilon_4=1$, and then $\epsilon_2=1$ by \ref{th:nozero}. If $(A,C)(t)=(\vartheta_4^4,\vartheta_2^4)(\tau(t))$, then \eqref{eq:modblock} and Lemma~\ref{lem:modcanon} would give $\vartheta_4^4(E_2+\vartheta_4^4+2\vartheta_2^4)=\vartheta_4^4(E_2-2\vartheta_2^4-\vartheta_4^4)$ along $\tau(t)$, that is $2\vartheta_2^4+\vartheta_4^4=0$, which is false since the left side has average one. Hence $(A,C)(t)=(\vartheta_2^4,\vartheta_4^4)(\tau(t))$, which proves \eqref{eq:modselect}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:bloch}
Let $a_0,b_0,C_0\in\mathbb{C}$, $C_0\ne0$, and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:blochfamily}
