T_k(w,\tau)=C_0\,e^{\pi ia_0(2w+a_0\tau)}\,\theta_k(w+a_0\tau+b_0|\tau)\qquad(k=1,\dots,4),
\end{equation}
$\Delta=\pi^{-1}\partial_wT_1$, $U=1/T_1$, $p_k=\vartheta_k(\tau)^2$ and $H=E_2(\tau)/12$. Then, wherever $T_1\ne0$, the vector $\mathbf J(w,\tau)$ satisfies $\pi^{-1}\partial_w\mathbf J=\mathcal Z(\mathbf J)$ and $(\pi i)^{-1}\partial_\tau\mathbf J=\Phi(\mathbf J)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:R12}
R_1:=p_2T_4^2-p_4T_2^2-p_3T_1^2=0,\qquad R_2:=p_2T_3^2-p_3T_2^2-p_4T_1^2=0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, along \eqref{eq:tauw}, $t\mapsto\mathbf J(w(t),\tau(t))$ solves \eqref{eq:jacblock} wherever $T_1\ne0$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Write $\xi=w+a_0\tau+b_0$ and $S(w,\tau)=C_0e^{\pi ia_0(2w+a_0\tau)}$, so $T_k=S\,\theta_k(\xi)$ and $\pi^{-1}\partial_wS=2ia_0S$. The relations \eqref{eq:R12} are \ref{J:quad} at $\xi$, multiplied by $S^2$. Since $T_\nu T_\mu/T_1^2=\theta_\nu\theta_\mu/\theta_1^2$ at $\xi$, \ref{J:brezhnev} gives $\pi^{-1}\partial_w(T_k/T_1)=-p_kT_\nu T_\mu/T_1^2$, which is equivalent to the second equation in \eqref{eq:Zfield}. Next, $\pi^{-1}\partial_wT_1=S(2ia_0\theta_1+\pi^{-1}\theta_1')$ and $\pi^{-2}\partial_w^2T_1=S(-4a_0^2\theta_1+4ia_0\pi^{-1}\theta_1'+\pi^{-2}\theta_1'')$, so $\pi^{-2}\partial_w^2T_1-(\pi^{-1}\partial_wT_1)^2/T_1=S(\pi^{-2}\theta_1''-\pi^{-2}\theta_1'^2/\theta_1)=-p_3p_4T_2^2/T_1-4\varkappa T_1$ by \ref{J:brezhnev}; this is the equation for $\mathcal Z\Delta$. The equations for $\mathcal ZT_1$ and $\mathcal ZU$ are definitions, and $\mathcal Zp_k=\mathcal ZH=0$ is clear.

For $\Phi$: the coefficient equations \eqref{eq:Phicoef} are the identities $D\vartheta_k^2=2\vartheta_k^2D\log\vartheta_k$ and \ref{th:ode}, rewritten with \ref{th:jacobi}. A direct computation shows that $f(w,\tau)=e^{2\pi iaw+\pi ia^2\tau}g(w+a\tau+b,\tau)$ satisfies $4\pi i\partial_\tau f=\partial_w^2f$ whenever $g$ does; hence by \ref{J:heat} each $T_k$ satisfies $(\pi i)^{-1}\partial_\tau T_k=-\frac14\pi^{-2}\partial_w^2T_k$, and so does $\Delta$. Computing $\pi^{-2}\partial_w^2T_k$ and $\pi^{-2}\partial_w^2\Delta$ with \eqref{eq:Zfield} (and $UT_1=1$) gives exactly \eqref{eq:Phijac}. The last assertion is the chain rule.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:thetafiber}
Let $\tau\in\mathbb{H}$, $p_k=\vartheta_k(\tau)^2$, and let $X_1,\dots,X_4\in\mathbb{C}$ with $X_1\ne0$ satisfy
\[
p_2X_4^2-p_4X_2^2-p_3X_1^2=0,\qquad p_2X_3^2-p_3X_2^2-p_4X_1^2=0.
\]
Then there are $\xi\in\mathbb{C}$ and $S\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ with $\theta_1(\xi|\tau)\ne0$ and $X_k=S\,\theta_k(\xi|\tau)$ for $k=1,\dots,4$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Put $f_k=\theta_k/\theta_1$ and $x_k=X_k/X_1$ for $k=2,3,4$. By \ref{J:period}, $f_4$ is a meromorphic function with periods $2$ and $\tau$, and by \ref{J:zeros} its poles in the period parallelogram spanned by $2$ and $\tau$ are the two simple zeros $0$ and $1$ of $\theta_1$. A nonconstant elliptic function takes every complex value as often, counted with multiplicity, as it has poles in a period parallelogram \cite[Chapter~7, \S2.4, Theorem~5 and the remark after it, p.~271]{Ahlfors}; hence there is $\xi_0$, not a pole, with $f_4(\xi_0)=x_4$. Dividing \ref{J:quad} by $\theta_1^2$ gives $p_2f_4^2-p_4f_2^2=p_3$ and $p_2f_3^2-p_3f_2^2=p_4$; comparing with the hypotheses, and using $p_k\ne0$ (\ref{th:nozero}), we get $x_2=\pm f_2(\xi_0)$ and then $x_3=\pm f_3(\xi_0)$. By \ref{J:period} and \ref{J:parity}, the map $\xi\mapsto1-\xi$ changes $(f_2,f_3,f_4)$ into $(-f_2,f_3,f_4)$, and $\xi\mapsto\xi+\tau$ changes it into $(-f_2,-f_3,f_4)$. Composing these maps we find $\xi$ with $(f_2,f_3,f_4)(\xi)=(x_2,x_3,x_4)$ and $\xi$ not a pole of $f_4$. Since $\theta_1$ and $\theta_4$ have no common zero, $\theta_1(\xi)\ne0$, and $S=X_1/\theta_1(\xi)$ works.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:jaccont}
Let $\mathbf J:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}^{10}$ be a solution of \eqref{eq:jacblock} such that, for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $p_k(t)=\vartheta_k(\tau(t))^2$ for $k=2,3,4$, $H(t)=E_2(\tau(t))/12$, $R_1=R_2=0$ and $UT_1=1$. Then there are $a_0,b_0,C_0\in\mathbb{C}$, $C_0\ne0$, such that $\mathbf J(t)$ is the vector of Lemma~\ref{lem:bloch} evaluated at $(w(t),\tau(t))$, for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:thetafiber} at $\tau(0)$ there are $\xi$ and $S\ne0$ with $T_k(0)=S\theta_k(\xi|\tau(0))$. Choose $a_0$ with $2ia_0=\Delta(0)/T_1(0)-\theta_1'(\xi)/(\pi\theta_1(\xi))$, then $b_0=\xi-w(0)-a_0\tau(0)$ and $C_0=Se^{-\pi ia_0(2w(0)+a_0\tau(0))}$. The vector $\tilde{\mathbf J}(t)$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:bloch} along \eqref{eq:tauw} then agrees with $\mathbf J(0)$ at $t=0$: the $T_k$ by construction, $\Delta$ by the computation of $\pi^{-1}\partial_wT_1$ in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:bloch}, and $U$ because $U(0)=1/T_1(0)$. Let $I$ be the largest open interval containing $0$ on which $\tilde T_1\ne0$ and $\tilde{\mathbf J}=\mathbf J$; it is nonempty by uniqueness of solutions of \eqref{eq:jacblock}, since $\tilde{\mathbf J}$ is a solution while $\tilde T_1\ne0$. If $I$ had a finite endpoint $t^*$, then $\tilde T_1,\dots,\tilde T_4,\tilde\Delta$ are continuous at $t^*$ (they are holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}$), so they agree with $\mathbf J$ at $t^*$; in particular $\tilde T_1(t^*)=T_1(t^*)\ne0$ because $U(t^*)T_1(t^*)=1$, hence $\tilde U=1/\tilde T_1$ is also continuous at $t^*$ and agrees with $U$ there. By uniqueness the two solutions agree on a neighborhood of $t^*$, contradicting maximality. Hence $I=\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:nonreal}
If $\operatorname{Im} a_0\ne0$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:jaccont}, then $|(T_1,\dots,T_4)(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Put $y_\lambda=\operatorname{Im}\tau_\lambda=\operatorname{Im}\tau(t)$ and $\xi(t)=w(t)+a_0\tau(t)+b_0$, an affine function of $t$ with $\operatorname{Im}\xi(t)=\operatorname{Im}(a_0)\Omega t/\pi+O(1)$. The prefactor in \eqref{eq:blochfamily} is the exponential of an affine function of $t$, so its logarithm has modulus $O(1+|t|)$. Write $\xi(t)=\xi_r(t)+n(t)\tau(t)$ with $n(t)\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|\operatorname{Im}\xi_r(t)|\le y_\lambda/2$; then $|n(t)|\ge c|t|-C$ for constants $c>0$, $C$. Iterating \ref{J:period} gives $|\theta_k(\xi_r+n\tau|\tau)|=e^{\pi n^2y_\lambda+2\pi n\operatorname{Im}\xi_r}|\theta_k(\xi_r|\tau)|\ge e^{\pi y_\lambda(n^2-|n|)}|\theta_k(\xi_r|\tau)|$. By \ref{J:period} the function $(\xi,\tau)\mapsto\max_k|\theta_k(\xi|\tau)|$ is invariant under $\xi\mapsto\xi+1$ and $\tau\mapsto\tau+2$, so on $\{|\operatorname{Im}\xi|\le y_\lambda/2,\ \operatorname{Im}\tau=y_\lambda\}$ it is bounded below by its minimum over a compact set, which is positive by \ref{J:zeros}. Hence $\log|(T_1,\dots,T_4)(t)|\ge\pi y_\lambda c^2t^2-O(1+|t|)\to\infty$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:threemoments}
In the situation of Proposition~\ref{prop:jaccont}, suppose that $\mathbf J$ is forward recurrent, that $N/\Omega\notin\mathbb{Q}$, and that $G$ is as above. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:threemoments}
\langle F\rangle=1,\qquad\langle Fe^{-i(\alpha+\beta)}\rangle=\lambda,\qquad\langle Fe^{-i(\alpha-\beta)}\rangle=\lambda,
\end{equation}
then $F(t)=\Theta_\lambda(e^{i\alpha(t)},e^{i\beta(t)})$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:nonreal} and recurrence, $a_0$ is real. Then \eqref{eq:Fbloch} is an absolutely convergent trigonometric series $F(t)=\sum_nd_ne^{i\nu_nt}$, where, with $x=n+a_0$ and $\varrho=N/\Omega$, the frequency is $\nu_n=\Omega x^2+Nx=\Omega x(x+\varrho)$ and $d_n=C'\lambda^{x^2}e^{2\pi inb_0}e^{ix^2\alpha_0+ix\beta_0}$. Averaging term by term, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:avg}, $\langle Fe^{-i\mu t}\rangle=\sum_{n:\nu_n=\mu}d_n$. The frequencies relevant for \eqref{eq:threemoments} are $\mu=0$, $\Omega+N$ and $\Omega-N$, and
\[
\nu=0\iff x\in\{0,-\varrho\},\qquad\nu=\Omega+N\iff x\in\{1,-1-\varrho\},\qquad\nu=\Omega-N\iff x\in\{-1,1-\varrho\}.
\]
Since $\varrho\notin\mathbb{Q}$, the set $a_0+\mathbb{Z}$ contains at most one element of each of these pairs, and since $\langle F\rangle=1\ne0$ it contains $0$ or $-\varrho$.

If $a_0\in\mathbb{Z}$, reindex so that $a_0=0$ (this changes $b_0$ and $C'$ only). The three averages give $d_0=C'=1$ and $d_1=\lambda e^{2\pi ib_0}e^{i(\alpha_0+\beta_0)}=\lambda e^{i(\alpha_0+\beta_0)}$, so $e^{2\pi ib_0}=1$ and $F=\Theta_\lambda(e^{i\alpha},e^{i\beta})$.

If $a_0\in-\varrho+\mathbb{Z}$, reindex so that $a_0=-\varrho$. Writing $x=n-\varrho$, the coefficients take the form $d_n=c_*R^{n^2}S^n$ with $R=\lambda e^{i\alpha_0}$ and constants $c_*,S\ne0$, while the frequencies are $\nu_n=\Omega n^2-Nn$. The averages give $d_0=c_*=1$ and $d_{-1}=RS^{-1}=\lambda e^{i(\alpha_0+\beta_0)}$, so $S=e^{-i\beta_0}$. Hence $d_n=\lambda^{n^2}e^{in^2\alpha_0-in\beta_0}$ and
\[
F(t)=\sum_n\lambda^{n^2}e^{in^2\alpha_0-in\beta_0}e^{i(n^2\Omega-nN)t}=\sum_k\lambda^{k^2}e^{ik^2\alpha(t)+ik\beta(t)}=\Theta_\lambda(e^{i\alpha(t)},e^{i\beta(t)}),
\]
after the substitution $k=-n$. (The reflected class $a_0\in-\varrho+\mathbb{Z}$ is the symmetry $x\mapsto-\varrho-x$ of the dispersion relation $\nu=\Omega x(x+\varrho)$ and gives the same function.)
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:zeroratio}
The irrationality of $\varrho=N/\Omega$ ensures that each pair of roots displayed in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:threemoments} contains at most one element of $a_0+\mathbb{Z}$. If $\varrho$ were an integer, this need not hold, and an average could see a sum of coefficients. If $\varrho=0$, which happens exactly when the $j$-th column of $B$ vanishes, the last two averages in \eqref{eq:threemoments} of the intended function $\Theta_\lambda$ itself are not $\lambda$: they see $d_1+d_{-1}$, and equal $\lambda(1+e^{\mp2i\beta_0})$. The nonresonance hypothesis avoids these collisions. This is why the construction of Lemma~\ref{lem:template} makes every column of $B$ nonzero; then $\varrho\notin\mathbb{Q}$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:irrational}, and the canonical averages are those of Lemma~\ref{lem:graph}(c).
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:selector}
Let $x:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_s}$ be a solution of $\dot x=X_e(x)$ such that

    \color@endgroup

  \enit@outeritem every moment has average zero along $x$;
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip

  \egroup

Then there are $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{q+r}$, $\varphi(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{q+r}$ and $R_0\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|R_0|=1$ such that, with $\omega=(\epsilon_\ell\sqrt{p_\ell})_\ell$ and $\varphi(t)=\varphi(0)+\omega t$, we have $\zeta_\ell(t)=e^{i\varphi_\ell(t)}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:selected}
F_j(t)=\Theta_\lambda(Q_j(t),V_j(t)),\qquad G^\pm_j(t)=(1-\eta W_j(t)^{\pm1})^{-1},\qquad\mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e(x(t))=R_0\,\mathfrak D_e(\varphi(t))
\end{equation}
for all $j$ and all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, where $\mathfrak D_e$ is the detector \eqref{eq:detector}.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Projections of a forward recurrent solution to subsystems are forward recurrent, and every component of $x$ has modulus at most $|x|$; so each block satisfies the hypotheses (ii) and (iv).

\emph{Clocks.} By (i) and Lemma~\ref{lem:controller}, every controller is at an equilibrium with $\omega_\ell=\epsilon_\ell\sqrt{p_\ell}$, and $\zeta_\ell(t)=e^{i\varphi_\ell(t)}$ for a continuous $\varphi_\ell(t)=\varphi_\ell(0)+\omega_\ell t$. Then $Q_j(t)=e^{i\alpha_j(t)}$ and $V_j(t)=e^{i\beta_j(t)}$ with $\alpha_j=4\varphi_j$, $\beta_j=4\sum_lB_{lj}\varphi_{q+l}$, so $\dot\alpha_j=\Omega_j$ and $\dot\beta_j=N_j$, and $\Omega_j\ne0$, $N_j/\Omega_j\notin\mathbb{Q}$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:irrational}. By \eqref{eq:oscgraph}, $R(t)=R_0\prod_l\chi_l(t)^{-c_l(e)}$ with $|R_0|=|R(0)|=1$.

\emph{Modular block.} Fix $j$ and put $\tau_j(t)=\tau_\lambda+\alpha_j(t)/\pi$. The averages of the first two moments in \eqref{eq:moments} are $\langle Y_j\rangle=1$ and $\langle Y_je^{-i\alpha_j}\rangle=2\lambda$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:modselect} gives $\mathbf m_j(t)=\mathbf m^{\mathrm{can}}(\tau_j(t))$. By the residuals, $p_{4,j}^2=\vartheta_4^4(\tau_j)$, so $p_{4,j}(t)/\vartheta_4^2(\tau_j(t))$ is a continuous function with values $\pm1$, hence constant; since $\vartheta_4^2(\tau_j(t))$ has average one and $\langle p_{4,j}\rangle=1$, we get $p_{4,j}=\vartheta_4^2(\tau_j)$. Similarly $p_{2,j}=\pm\vartheta_2^2(\tau_j)$ with a constant sign. Now
\[
\vartheta_2^2(\tau)=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{\pi i\tau((m+\frac12)^2+(n+\frac12)^2)},
\]
and $e^{\pi i\tau_j(t)\sigma}=\lambda^\sigma e^{4i\sigma\varphi_j(t)}$; the smallest exponent $\sigma=\frac12$ occurs for four pairs $(m,n)$, and $\bar\zeta_j^2=e^{-2i\varphi_j}$. Hence $\vartheta_2^2(\tau_j)\bar\zeta_j^2$ has average $4\lambda^{1/2}=\frac14$, and $\langle p_{2,j}\bar\zeta_j^2\rangle=\frac14$ forces $p_{2,j}=\vartheta_2^2(\tau_j)$. Finally $p_{3,j}=Y_j^2=\vartheta_3^2(\tau_j)$ and $H_j=E_j/12=E_2(\tau_j)/12$.

\emph{Jacobi block.} With $\alpha=\alpha_j$, $\beta=\beta_j$, $\tau=\tau_j$ and $w$ as in \eqref{eq:tauw}, the block $\mathbf J_j$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:jaccont}, by the previous step and (i). The coordinate $G_j$ satisfies $G_j^4=\lambda Q_jV_j^2=\lambda e^{i\alpha+2i\beta}$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:threemoments}, applied with the last three moments in \eqref{eq:moments}, gives $F_j(t)=\Theta_\lambda(e^{i\alpha_j(t)},e^{i\beta_j(t)})=\Theta_\lambda(Q_j(t),V_j(t))$.

\emph{Reciprocals and detector.} Since $|W_j|=1$ and $\eta<1$, $1-\eta W_j^{\pm1}\ne0$, and the residuals give $G^\pm_j=(1-\eta W_j^{\pm1})^{-1}$; thus $(1-\eta^2)G^+_jG^-_j=P_\eta(W_j)=P_\eta(Q_j^{-1}S_j)$ by \eqref{eq:ThetaP}. Substituting everything into \eqref{eq:detobs} and comparing with \eqref{eq:detector} gives the last identity in \eqref{eq:selected}.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:yes}
If $e\in K$, there is no solution $x$ of $\dot x=X_e(x)$ satisfying (i)--(iv) of Theorem~\ref{thm:selector} and $\langle \mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e(x)\rangle=0$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:selector}, $\mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e(x(t))=R_0\mathfrak D_e(\varphi_0+\omega t)$. The Fourier series of $\mathfrak D_e$ converges absolutely (Lemma~\ref{lem:constterm}) and $k\cdot\omega\ne0$ for $k\ne0$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:irrational}), so Lemma~\ref{lem:avg} gives $\langle \mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e(x)\rangle=R_0\sum_{n}(\lambda\eta)^{|n|^2}$, the sum being over the solutions of \eqref{eq:template}. This is nonzero for $e\in K$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:constterm}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->

    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem every validity residual vanishes on the image of $\Gamma_e$;
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
   
    \unskip
    \xdef\enit@afteritem{ 
      \ifhmode\spacefactor\the\spacefactor\relax\fi} 
    \color@endgroup
  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem every coordinate of $h_e\circ\Gamma_e$ has an absolutely convergent Fourier series on $\mathbb{T}^{q+r}$; the constant terms of the moments are zero, and the constant term of $\mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e\circ\Gamma_e=\mathfrak D_e$ is \eqref{eq:constterm}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Every coordinate is a series in the characters $e^{ik\cdot\varphi}$ with integer vectors $k$: for instance $e^{\pi i\tau_j(n+1/2)^2}=\lambda^{(n+1/2)^2}e^{i(4n^2+4n+1)\varphi_j}$, and $\theta_1(w_j|\tau_j)$ involves $e^{i(4n^2+8n+3)\varphi_j}$ and $e^{2i(2n+1)\sum_lB_{lj}\varphi_{q+l}}$. Hence $\Gamma_e$ is $2\pi$-periodic in each $\varphi_\ell$. (a) The controllers are at equilibria and $\dot\varphi=\omega$; the modular blocks solve \eqref{eq:modblock} by Lemma~\ref{lem:modcanon}; the Jacobi blocks are the case $a_0=b_0=0$, $C_0=1$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:bloch}; the remaining coordinates are explicit characters or rational functions of characters, and satisfy \eqref{eq:oscillator} and \eqref{eq:source} by direct differentiation. (b) The residuals \eqref{eq:residuals} vanish by \ref{th:jacobi}, \ref{J:quad} and the definitions. (c) Every coordinate is a finite product of characters, of absolutely convergent theta series in characters (for $\theta_1'$ the coefficients acquire a polynomial factor, which does not affect absolute convergence), and of the geometric series $(1-\eta W^{\pm1})^{-1}$ and $1/\Theta_\lambda=\sum_{m\ge0}(1-\Theta_\lambda)^m$; products of absolutely convergent Fourier series converge absolutely. For the moments: the constant term of $Y_j=\vartheta_3(\tau_j)=1+2\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^{n^2}e^{4in^2\varphi_j}$ is $1$, and that of $Y_j\bar Q_j$ is $2\lambda$; the constant term of $\vartheta_4^2(\tau_j)$ is $1$, and that of $\vartheta_2^2(\tau_j)\bar\zeta_j^2$ is $\frac14$, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:selector}; and $F_j=\sum_n\lambda^{n^2}Q_j^{n^2}V_j^n$, where $Q_j^{n^2}V_j^n=e^{4in^2\varphi_j+4in\sum_lB_{lj}\varphi_{q+l}}$, so the constant terms of $F_j$, $F_j\bar Q_j\bar V_j$ and $F_j\bar Q_jV_j$ come from $n=0$, $n=1$ and $n=-1$ respectively (here $B_j\ne0$ is used), and equal $1$, $\lambda$ and $\lambda$. The last assertion holds because $\mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e\circ\Gamma_e=\mathfrak D_e$.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:central}
$\widehat X$ and $\hat g$ are polynomials with rational coefficients if $X$ and $g$ have rational coefficients, and $\widehat X$ is tangent to $S^n$. The equator $\{w=0\}$ is invariant. On each open hemisphere $\pm w>0$, the map $(y,w)\mapsto x=y/w$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb{R}^n$ which sends $\widehat X$ to $(1+|x|^2)^{-M/2}X(x)$, and $\hat g=(1+|x|^2)^{-M/2}g(x)$ and $w^2=(1+|x|^2)^{-1}$ there.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
A monomial of degree $d\le M$ in $y/w$ multiplied by $w^{M+1}$ or $w^{M+2}$ is a polynomial, and so is $w^M$ times it. On $S^n$, $\frac{d}{d\sigma}(|y|^2+w^2)=2w^{M+1}(y\cdot X)(1-|y|^2-w^2)=0$. The component $\widehat X_w$ is divisible by $w$. On a hemisphere, $x=y/w$ satisfies $\frac{dx}{d\sigma}=\widehat X_y/w-y\widehat X_w/w^2=w^MX(x)$, and $|y|^2+w^2=1$ gives $w^2=(1+|x|^2)^{-1}$; since $M$ is even, $w^M=(1+|x|^2)^{-M/2}$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:selectedorbit}
Let $\nu_0$ be an ergodic invariant probability measure of the flow of $\widehat X_e$ on $S^{n_s}$ with $\nu_0(\{w\ne0\})=1$ and $\int\hat h_e\,d\nu_0=0$. Then there is a solution $x:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_s}$ of $\dot x=X_e(x)$ which satisfies (i)--(iv) of Theorem~\ref{thm:selector} with $\mu=M$, and along which $\langle h_e(x)\rangle=0$.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Write $\phi_\sigma$ for the flow of $\widehat X_e$, $f=w^M$ and $a=\int f\,d\nu_0>0$. Each validity residual $v$ is a coordinate of $h_e$ and $v\ge0$, so $\hat v=fv(y/w)\ge0$ and $\int\hat v\,d\nu_0=0$ give $\hat v=0$ $\nu_0$-almost everywhere. By Fubini's theorem, for $\nu_0$-almost every $p$ the open set $\{\sigma:\hat v(\phi_\sigma p)>0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero, hence is empty. By \ref{E:birkhoff} and \ref{E:poincare} we may therefore choose $p_0$ with $w(p_0)\ne0$ such that: $p_0$ is forward recurrent; $\hat v(\phi_\sigma p_0)=0$ for all $\sigma$ and all validity residuals $v$; $\frac1\sigma\int_0^\sigma f(\phi_sp_0)ds\to a$ as $\sigma\to\pm\infty$; and $\frac1\sigma\int_0^\sigma\hat h_e(\phi_sp_0)ds\to0$ as $\sigma\to+\infty$. The orbit of $p_0$ stays in the open hemisphere containing $p_0$. The function $t(\sigma)=\int_0^\sigma f(\phi_sp_0)\,ds$ is increasing with $t(\sigma)/\sigma\to a>0$ as $\sigma\to\pm\infty$, so it is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:central} the function $x$ defined by $x(t(\sigma))=y(\phi_\sigma p_0)/w(\phi_\sigma p_0)$ solves $\dot x=X_e(x)$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Property (i) holds because $v(x)=\hat v/f$. If $\phi_{\sigma_k}p_0\to p_0$ with $\sigma_k\to\infty$, then $x(t(\sigma_k))\to x(0)$, which is (ii). By the change of variables $dt=f\,d\sigma$ and $\hat h_e=fh_e(x)$,
\[
\frac1{t(\sigma)}\int_0^{t(\sigma)}h_e(x)\,dt=\frac{\sigma}{t(\sigma)}\cdot\frac1\sigma\int_0^\sigma\hat h_e(\phi_sp_0)\,ds\to0,\qquad\frac1{t(\sigma)}\int_0^{t(\sigma)}(1+|x|^2)^{M/2}dt=\frac{\sigma}{t(\sigma)}\to\frac1a,
\]
which gives (iii), $\langle h_e(x)\rangle=0$, and (iv).
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:accumulator}
Let $\phi$ be a continuous flow on a compact metric space $\mathcal{K}_0$, $g:\mathcal{K}_0\to\mathbb{R}^m$ continuous, and consider on $\mathcal{K}_0\times S^m$ the skew product $\dot u=(1+u_0)g-(u\cdot g)u$, $\dot u_0=-(1+u_0)(u\cdot g)$ over $\phi$. If $\nu_0\in\mathcal{M}(\phi)$ is ergodic and $\int g\,d\nu_0\ne0$, then every invariant probability measure $\nu$ of the skew product whose projection to $\mathcal{K}_0$ is $\nu_0$ satisfies $\nu(\{u_0=-1\})=1$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The set $E=\{u_0\ne-1\}$ is invariant, since its complement $\mathcal{K}_0\times\{(0,-1)\}$ is. Suppose $\nu(E)>0$, and let $\nu'=\nu(\cdot\cap E)/\nu(E)$, an invariant probability measure. Its projection to $\mathcal{K}_0$ is at most $\nu_0/\nu(E)$, so the set $\mathcal G$ of points $b$ with $\frac1\sigma\int_0^\sigma g(\phi_sb)\,ds\to\bar g:=\int g\,d\nu_0$, which has full $\nu_0$-measure by \ref{E:birkhoff}, has full measure for this projection. By \ref{E:poincare} there is a forward recurrent point $p\in E$ of the skew product whose projection lies in $\mathcal G$. Along its orbit $z=u/(1+u_0)$ satisfies $z(\sigma)-z(0)=\int_0^\sigma g(\phi_sb)\,ds$, so $|z(\sigma)|/\sigma\to|\bar g|>0$, hence $(u,u_0)(\sigma)\to(0,-1)$ as $\sigma\to\infty$, contradicting recurrence to $p\in E$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounds}
There are rational numbers $M_0\ge1$ and $K_0>0$, which do not depend on $e$, with the following properties. Put $M_e=M_0$ and $K_e=K_0\rho_*^{4D_h|c(e)|_1}$. First, $|\Gamma_e(\varphi)|^2\le M_e$ for all $\varphi$. Second, the function
\begin{equation}\label{eq:primitive}
\mathcal B_e(\varphi)=\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{\hat h_k}{i\,k\cdot\omega}\,e^{ik\cdot\varphi},\qquad\text{where }h_e\circ\Gamma_e=\sum_k\hat h_ke^{ik\cdot\varphi},
\end{equation}
is continuous and real-valued, satisfies $|\mathcal B_e|\le K_e$, and $\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal B_e(\varphi+\omega t)=h_e(\Gamma_e(\varphi+\omega t))-\hat h_0$. If $e\notin K$, then $\hat h_0=0$.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: the coordinates of $\Gamma_e$.} All coordinates of $\Gamma_e$ except $R$ are independent of $e$; we show that they have finite $\|\cdot\|_{\rho_*}$. The controllers are constants, and $\zeta_\ell$ and $G_j$ are constant multiples of characters. Since $e^{\pi i\tau_j\sigma}=\lambda^\sigma e^{4i\sigma\varphi_j}$, the theta constants and $E_2$ at $\tau_j$ are series $\sum_nc_n\lambda^{\sigma_n}e^{4i\sigma_n\varphi_j}$ in which $|c_n|$ grows at most polynomially and $\sigma_n\ge0$ grows at least linearly in $|n|$; as $\lambda\rho_*^4<1$, their norms are finite, and so are those of the coordinates of $\mathbf m_j$, of the $p_{k,j}$ and of $H_j$, which are products of them. Since $w_j=z_j+\frac{1+\tau_j}2$ and $\pi z_j=2\sum_lB_{lj}\varphi_{q+l}$, the $n$-th term of each of $T_{1,j},\dots,T_{4,j},\Delta_j$ has the form $c\,\lambda^{\sigma}e^{ik\cdot\varphi}$ with $|c|\le4(2|n|+1)$, $\sigma\ge0$ a quadratic polynomial in $n$, and $|k|_1\le4\sigma+1+2(2|n|+1)|B|_1$; again the norms are finite because $\lambda\rho_*^4<1$. Since $|n|\le n^2$, \eqref{eq:rhochoice} gives
\[
\|1-\Theta_\lambda(Q_j,V_j)\|_{\rho_*}\le\sum_{n\ne0}\lambda^{n^2}\rho_*^{4n^2+4|n||B|_1}\le2\sum_{n\ge1}8^{-n}=\tfrac27,
\]
so $\|1/\Theta_\lambda(Q_j,V_j)\|_{\rho_*}\le\frac75$, and $U_j=G_j/\Theta_\lambda(Q_j,V_j)$ (by \ref{J:half}) has finite norm. Finally $G^\pm_j=\sum_{m\ge0}\eta^mW_j^{\pm m}$ with $W_j=e^{-4i\varphi_j+4i\sum_lA_{lj}\varphi_{q+l}}$, so $\|G^\pm_j\|_{\rho_*}\le\sum_m(\eta\rho_*^{4+4|A|_1})^m\le\sum_m(\tfrac34)^m=4$. On the other hand $R=e^{-4i\sum_lc_l(e)\varphi_{q+l}}$ has $|R|=1$ and $\|R\|_{\rho_*}=\rho_*^{4|c(e)|_1}$. Since $\|\operatorname{Re} f\|_{\rho_*}$, $\|\operatorname{Im} f\|_{\rho_*}\le\|f\|_{\rho_*}$, there is a real $\Lambda\ge1$, independent of $e$, such that every real coordinate of $\Gamma_e$ has norm at most $\Lambda$, except the real and imaginary parts of $R$, which have norm at most $\rho_*^{4|c(e)|_1}$. As $\sup|f|\le\|f\|_{\rho_*}$, any rational $M_0\ge n_s\Lambda^2$ satisfies $|\Gamma_e|^2\le M_0$.

\emph{Step 2: the drift.} The coordinates $h_{e,i}$ of $h_e$ are polynomials of degree at most $D_h$ whose coefficients do not depend on $e$. Let $c_h$ be the sum of the absolute values of all their coefficients. By Step~1 and the properties of $\|\cdot\|_{\rho_*}$, every monomial of degree at most $D_h$ in the coordinates of $\Gamma_e$ has norm at most $\Lambda^{D_h}\rho_*^{4D_h|c(e)|_1}$, so
\[
\sum_i\|h_{e,i}\circ\Gamma_e\|_{\rho_*}\le c_h\Lambda^{D_h}\rho_*^{4D_h|c(e)|_1}.
\]

\emph{Step 3: the primitive.} Let $\hat h_{k,i}$ be the Fourier coefficients of $h_{e,i}\circ\Gamma_e$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:radicals} with $s=2^d-1$ and $P=p_d$, $|k\cdot\omega|^{-1}\le P^{s/2}|k|_1^s$ for $k\ne0$, and for $n\ge1$ we have $n^s\rho_*^{-n}\le(sm_*)^s$ (for $n\ge s$ because $\rho_*^n\ge\binom ns m_*^{-s}\ge(n/s)^sm_*^{-s}$). Hence, using that the Euclidean norm of a vector is at most the sum of the absolute values of its coordinates,
\[
|\mathcal B_e(\varphi)|\le\sum_i\sum_{k\ne0}\frac{|\hat h_{k,i}|}{|k\cdot\omega|}\le P^{s/2}(sm_*)^s\sum_i\sum_k|\hat h_{k,i}|\rho_*^{|k|_1}\le P^{s/2}(sm_*)^sc_h\Lambda^{D_h}\rho_*^{4D_h|c(e)|_1},
\]
and any rational $K_0\ge P^{s/2}(sm_*)^sc_h\Lambda^{D_h}$ works. In particular \eqref{eq:primitive} converges absolutely and uniformly, so $\mathcal B_e$ is continuous, and termwise differentiation, justified by the absolute convergence of $\sum_k|\hat h_k|$, gives the derivative along the flow. Since $h_e$ is real, $\hat h_{-k}=\overline{\hat h_k}$, so $\mathcal B_e$ is real-valued. If $e\notin K$, then $\hat h_0=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:graph}(b),(c) and Lemma~\ref{lem:constterm}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:signgap}
Let $\beta_e=\beta(\Psi_e,\mathcal{R}_e)$ be the maximal invariant average of the reward $\mathcal{R}_e$ for the flow $\Psi_e$ of \eqref{eq:compactsource} on $\mathcal{K}$. If $e\in K$, then $\beta_e\le-\varepsilon_e<0$. If $e\notin K$, then $\beta_e\ge\frac54w_e^*>0$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let $e\in K$. By \ref{E:decomp} it suffices to show $\int\mathcal{R}_e\,d\nu\le-\varepsilon_e$ for every ergodic $\nu\in\mathcal{M}(\Psi_e)$. The projection $\nu_0$ of $\nu$ to $S^{n_s}$ is an ergodic invariant measure for $\widehat X_e$ by \ref{E:factor}, and the equator $\{w=0\}$ is invariant, so $\nu_0(\{w=0\})\in\{0,1\}$. If it is $1$, then $w^2=0$ and $u_0\le1$ give $\mathcal{R}_e\le-\varepsilon_e$ $\nu$-almost everywhere. Otherwise $\nu_0(\{w\ne0\})=1$. If $\int\hat h_e\,d\nu_0=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:selectedorbit} gives a solution of $\dot x=X_e(x)$ satisfying (i)--(iv) of Theorem~\ref{thm:selector} with $\langle h_e(x)\rangle=0$, and in particular $\langle \mathfrak D^{\mathrm{obs}}_e(x)\rangle=0$; this contradicts Corollary~\ref{cor:yes}. Hence $\int\kappa_e\hat h_e\,d\nu_0\ne0$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:accumulator} gives $u_0=-1$ $\nu$-almost everywhere, where $\mathcal{R}_e=2w^2-2-\varepsilon_e\le-\varepsilon_e$.

Let $e\notin K$. Consider the set $\widehat\Gamma_e\subseteq\mathcal{K}$ of points with $w>0$, $y/w=\Gamma_e(\varphi)$ and $u/(1+u_0)=\kappa_e\mathcal B_e(\varphi)$ for some $\varphi\in\mathbb{T}^d$. It is compact, as a continuous image of $\mathbb{T}^d$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:graph}(a) and Lemma~\ref{lem:bounds} (with $\hat h_0=0$), $t\mapsto(\Gamma_e(\varphi+\omega t),\kappa_e\mathcal B_e(\varphi+\omega t))$ solves the skew product \eqref{eq:skew}; since $w^M\ge(w_e^*)^{M/2}>0$ on $\widehat\Gamma_e$, the time $t$ of the original system runs over all of $\mathbb{R}$ along each orbit of $\Psi_e$ in $\widehat\Gamma_e$, so $\widehat\Gamma_e$ is invariant. On $\widehat\Gamma_e$ we have $w^2=(1+|\Gamma_e|^2)^{-1}\ge w_e^*$ and, with $|z|=\kappa_e|\mathcal B_e|\le\kappa_eK_e$ and $\kappa_e^2K_e^2\le w_e^*/4$,
\[
u_0=\frac{1-|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}\ge1-2|z|^2\ge1-\frac{w_e^*}2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\mathcal{R}_e\ge1-\frac{w_e^*}2+2w_e^*-1-\frac{w_e^*}4=\frac54w_e^*.
\]
By \ref{E:compact} applied to the restriction of $\Psi_e$ to $\widehat\Gamma_e$, there is an invariant probability measure supported on $\widehat\Gamma_e$, and its reward average is at least $\frac54w_e^*$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:wrapper}
Let $k\ge1$, $n_1,\dots,n_k\ge1$, $\mathcal{K}=S^{n_1-1}\times\dots\times S^{n_k-1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_1}\times\dots\times\mathbb{R}^{n_k}$, let $P=(P_1,\dots,P_k)$ be a polynomial vector field with rational coefficients which is tangent to $\mathcal{K}$ at every point of $\mathcal{K}$, and let $a$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients. Let $D\ge3$ be odd with $D\ge\deg P$ and $D-1\ge\deg a$, and put $L=k+1$ and $E=D+2L$. Then one can compute from $(P,a,D)$ a homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^{1+n_1+\dots+n_k}$ of degree $E$ with rational coefficients such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wrapper}
0\text{ is GAS for }\dot v=F(v)\iff\beta(P|_\mathcal{K},a)<0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Write $v=(v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k)=(z,x_1,\dots,x_k)$ with $z\in\mathbb{R}$, $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}$, and put $s_i=|v_i|^2$ and $|v|^2=\sum_{i=0}^ks_i$. Define the homogeneous polynomials
\[
\Pi_0=0,\qquad\Pi_i(v)=z^DP_i(x/z)\ (1\le i\le k),\qquad\alpha(v)=z^{D-1}a(x/z),
\]
of degrees $D$ and $D-1$. Put
\[
T_i=s_i\Pi_i-v_i(v_i\cdot\Pi_i),\qquad\bar f(s)=\frac1L\sum_{j=0}^ks_j(1-s_j),\qquad N_i=(1-s_i-\bar f(s))v_i,\qquad\mathcal B=T+N,
\]
and $\mathcal H=\prod_{i=0}^ks_i$, $b=\mathcal H\alpha-(1-\mathcal H)$. We have $v_i\cdot T_i=0$, so $\frac d{dt}s_i=2v_i\cdot N_i=2s_i(1-s_i-\bar f)$ along $\dot v=\mathcal B(v)$, and $v\cdot\mathcal B(v)=\sum_is_i(1-s_i)-\bar f|v|^2$, which vanishes on the sphere $S_L=\{|v|^2=L\}$. Thus $\mathcal B$ is tangent to $S_L$.

\emph{Invariant measures on $S_L$.} Put $\Phi(s)=\sum_{i=0}^k(s_i-\frac12s_i^2)$. On $S_L$, using $\sum_is_i(1-s_i-\bar f)=0$,
\[
\frac d{dt}\Phi=\sum_i2s_i(1-s_i)(1-s_i-\bar f)=2\sum_is_i(1-s_i-\bar f)^2\ge0,
\]
with equality exactly when there is a nonempty $I\subseteq\{0,\dots,k\}$ with $s_i=L/|I|$ for $i\in I$ and $s_i=0$ for $i\notin I$. Each such set $Z_I\subseteq S_L$ is compact and invariant, since $\dot s=0$ on it. For $\nu\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal B|_{S_L})$, \ref{E:deriv} gives $\int\dot\Phi\,d\nu=0$, so $\nu$ is supported on the finite union of the $Z_I$, and $\nu$ is a convex combination of invariant probability measures on the individual $Z_I$. If $I\ne\{0,\dots,k\}$, then $\mathcal H=0$ and $b=-1$ on $Z_I$. On $Z_{\{0,\dots,k\}}=\{z=\pm1\}\times\mathcal{K}$ we have $\bar f=0$, so $\dot z=0$, and for $y=x/z\in\mathcal{K}$ tangency gives $x_i\cdot\Pi_i=z^{D+1}y_i\cdot P_i(y)=0$, so $\dot x_i=\Pi_i=z^DP_i(y)$ and $\dot y=z^{D-1}P(y)=P(y)$, because $D-1$ is even. Likewise $b=\alpha=a(y)$ there. So on each of the two sheets $z=\pm1$ the flow of $\mathcal B$ with the function $b$ is conjugate to the flow of $P$ on $\mathcal{K}$ with the function $a$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wrapperavg}
\beta(\mathcal B|_{S_L},b)=\max\{\beta(P|_\mathcal{K},a),-1\},
\end{equation}
the value $-1$ being attained, for instance, at the equilibria $(\pm\sqrt L,0,\dots,0)\in Z_{\{0\}}$. In particular $\beta(\mathcal B|_{S_L},b)<0$ if and only if $\beta(P|_\mathcal{K},a)<0$.

\emph{Homogenization.} The components of $T$ are homogeneous of degree $D+2$ and those of $N$ are sums of homogeneous pieces of degrees $1,3,5$; the pieces of $b$ have degrees $0$, $2L$ and $2L+D-1$. Since $L\ge2$, all degrees in $\mathcal B$ are odd and at most $E$, and all degrees in $b$ are even and at most $E-1$. For a polynomial $G=\sum_\ell G_\ell$, with $G_\ell$ homogeneous of degree $\ell$, $\ell\le e$ and $\ell\equiv e\pmod2$, put $\mathrm{Hom}_e(G)=\sum_\ell(|v|^2/L)^{(e-\ell)/2}G_\ell$; it is homogeneous of degree $e$, has rational coefficients, and equals $G$ on $S_L$. Define
\[
Y=\mathrm{Hom}_E(\mathcal B),\qquad\mathcal A=\mathrm{Hom}_{E-1}(b),\qquad F(v)=Y(v)+\mathcal A(v)\,v.
\]
Then $F$ is homogeneous of degree $E$ with rational coefficients. The polynomial $v\cdot Y(v)$ is homogeneous and vanishes on $S_L$, hence vanishes identically. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:gascrit} with $Q(v)=|v|^2/L$, so that $S_Q=S_L$: on $S_L$ we get $a_F=v\cdot F/L=\mathcal A=b$ and $Y_F=F-a_Fv=Y=\mathcal B$. Hence the origin is GAS for $F$ if and only if $\beta(\mathcal B|_{S_L},b)<0$, which by \eqref{eq:wrapperavg} proves \eqref{eq:wrapper}. All steps are finite operations on rational polynomials.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
The reduction $e\mapsto F_e$ is the composition of the following finite steps, all of which use only rational arithmetic and the fixed integer tables $A,B,c_0,c_1$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:template}.

  \enit@outeritem Compute $c(e)=c_0+ec_1$ and write down the source vector field $X_e$ of Section~\ref{sec:source}, realified, and the drift $h_e$. Only the coefficients of the oscillator equation \eqref{eq:oscillator} depend on $e$.
 
    \unskip

  \enit@outeritem Compute $M_e$, $K_e$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:bounds} and $\kappa_e,\varepsilon_e$ by \eqref{eq:kappaeps}.

  \egroup
  \enit@outeritem Write down the vector field \eqref{eq:compactsource} on $\mathcal{K}=S^{n_s}\times S^{n_h}$ and the reward \eqref{eq:reward}.
 
    \unskip
    \xdef\relax{

  \enit@outeritem Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:wrapper} with $k=2$, $n_1=n_s+1$, $n_2=n_h+1$, and $D=M+3$.
\end{enumerate}
The numbers $n_s$, $n_h$ and $M$ do not depend on $e$, and the degree of \eqref{eq:compactsource} is at most $M+3$, which does not depend on $e$ either. Since $M$ is even and the reward has degree two, this choice of $D$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:wrapper}. Hence the dimension $N_*=1+(n_s+1)+(n_h+1)$ and the odd degree $d_*=D+6$ of $F_e$ do not depend on $e$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:signgap} and Theorem~\ref{thm:wrapper},
\[
e\in K\iff\beta_e<0\iff0\text{ is GAS for }\dot x=F_e(x).
\]
The map $e\mapsto F_e$ is total and computable and never tests whether $e\in K$; so it is a many-one reduction from $K$ to $\mathrm{HGAS}(N_*,d_*)$, and $\mathrm{HGAS}(N_*,d_*)$ is many-one hard by \ref{C:K} and \ref{C:trans}. It is r.e.\ by Proposition~\ref{prop:re}.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Let $N_*$ and $d_*=2k_*+1$ be given by Theorem~\ref{thm:fixedpair}, so that $\mathrm{HGAS}(N_*,d_*)$ is many-one complete. By Corollary~\ref{cor:transfer} with $n_0=N_*$ and $k_0=k_*$, the set $\mathrm{HGAS}(N,d)$ is many-one complete for every $N\ge N_3:=\binom{N_*+k_*-1}{k_*}$ and every odd $d\ge3$. The remaining assertions follow from Section~\ref{subsec:computability}.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Adjoining the constants $N_*,d_*$ to a coefficient code is a computable map which reduces $\mathrm{HGAS}(N_*,d_*)$ to $\mathrm{HGAS}$, so $\mathrm{HGAS}$ is many-one hard by Theorem~\ref{thm:fixedpair}, and it is r.e.\ by Proposition~\ref{prop:re}. By Theorem~\ref{thm:normalform}(iii), $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,3)$ and $\mathrm{HGAS}(\cdot,d)$, $d\ge3$ odd, are many-one equivalent to $\mathrm{HGAS}$, hence many-one complete as well. Complements of many-one hard sets are not r.e.\ (Section~\ref{subsec:computability}).
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:radicals}
Let $p_1,\dots,p_d$ be distinct primes. For $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $m_S=\prod_{a\in S}p_a$, with $m_\emptyset=1$. Then the $2^d$ numbers $\sqrt{m_S}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. In particular $\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_d}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Let $F_d$ be the set of real numbers $\sum_Sc_S\sqrt{m_S}$ with $c_S\in\mathbb{Q}$. Since $\sqrt{m_S}\sqrt{m_T}=m_{S\cap T}\sqrt{m_{S\triangle T}}$, the set $F_d$ is closed under addition and multiplication. We prove by induction on $d$, for all choices of $d$ distinct primes, the following two statements: (a) the numbers $\sqrt{m_S}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$; (b) the inverse of every nonzero element of $F_d$ lies in $F_d$. For $d=0$ both are clear, since $F_0=\mathbb{Q}$.

Assume (a) and (b) for $d-1$ primes. By (a) for $p_1,\dots,p_{d-1}$, for each $a\le d-1$ the map $\sigma_a\bigl(\sum_Sc_S\sqrt{m_S}\bigr)=\sum_S(-1)^{[a\in S]}c_S\sqrt{m_S}$ is well defined on $F_{d-1}$; it is additive, multiplicative (check on products of basis elements, using $[a\in S\triangle T]\equiv[a\in S]+[a\in T]\bmod2$) and injective, and an element of $F_{d-1}$ is rational if and only if it is fixed by every $\sigma_a$.

\emph{$\sqrt{p_d}\notin F_{d-1}$.} Suppose $x=\sqrt{p_d}\in F_{d-1}$. Then $\sigma_a(x)^2=\sigma_a(p_d)=p_d$, so $\sigma_a(x)=\pm x$; let $A$ be the set of $a$ with $\sigma_a(x)=-x$. Since $\sigma_a(\sqrt{m_A})=-\sqrt{m_A}$ exactly for $a\in A$, the number $y=x\sqrt{m_A}\in F_{d-1}$ is fixed by every $\sigma_a$, hence rational. But $y=\sqrt{p_dm_A}$ and $p_d$ divides $p_dm_A$ exactly once, so $p_dm_A$ is not the square of an integer and $y$ is irrational by unique factorization, a contradiction.

\emph{(a) for $d$.} If $\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}}c_S\sqrt{m_S}=0$, collect the terms with $d\notin S$ and $d\in S$ to get $x+y\sqrt{p_d}=0$ with $x,y\in F_{d-1}$. If $y\ne0$, then $\sqrt{p_d}=-x/y\in F_{d-1}$ by (b) for $d-1$, which we have excluded. So $y=0$, hence $x=0$, and (a) for $d-1$ shows that all $c_S$ vanish.

\emph{(b) for $d$.} By (a) for $d$ the maps $\sigma_a$, now for $1\le a\le d$, are well-defined injective additive and multiplicative maps of $F_d$, and an element of $F_d$ fixed by all of them is rational. For $0\ne x\in F_d$, the product $\mathcal N(x)$ of the $2^d$ numbers obtained from $x$ by applying all compositions of the $\sigma_a$ is fixed by every $\sigma_a$, so it is rational, and it is nonzero because each factor is. Then $x^{-1}=\mathcal N(x)^{-1}\prod'\in F_d$, where $\prod'$ is the product of the factors other than $x$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
